                    a super-power that allows them to
                    travel between universes, but it’s hardly
                    unheard of. America Chavez, for instance,
                    can literally punch her way from one world
                    into another.

                                                                         10
                   NARRATOR
                    This chapter is meant for the Narrator, the person
                    who runs the sessions of the game for the rest of the players.
                    If you don’t plan to take on that vital role, you can skip over
                    this section entirely. There’s no need for you to read it. You
                    can just focus on picking or creating your character instead.
                        That said, there are no Narrator-exclusive secrets here
                    that regular players shouldn’t lay their eyes on. If you want
                    to read this chapter for any reason, go right ahead.
                        You don’t need to be a Narrator to be a good player, but
                    understanding the Narrator’s role can help you be a better
                    one. And if you decide that you want to take a crack at being
                    a Narrator at some point, then you would be all set to start.
                        If you are a Narrator—or plan to become one—then be
                    sure to read this chapter. This is the one part of the book
                    that’s entirely meant for you.
                    BEING THE NARRATOR
                    The Narrator has the most important role in the game. While
                    the other players take on the role of a single character, you
                    do that for every other character in the game, and you set
                    up the scenarios in which the characters find themselves.
                    On top of that, the Narrator provides the descriptions of
                    everything the characters see, touch, hear, smell, taste and
                    feel in the game—the totality of their experiences—and
                    you have the final call over any disagreements in the game
                    too, whether that’s about how the rules work or what the
                    results of an action or dice roll might be.
                       Of course—like any faithful Marvel fan—you know that
                    with great power there must also come great responsibility.
                       As the Narrator, you have the most control over the game.
                    You set up the scenarios, play most of the roles and ultimately
                                                                                      2
Michael Syrett (Order #53194700)
     have the most power. It can be a challenge to handle all
     that responsibility, but it’s also tremendously rewarding.
         The game isn’t about responsibilities, though. It’s about fun.
         It’s up to you to do your best to make sure that everyone
     playing in the game is having fun. Including you.
         First and foremost, do your best to set up a safe and
     welcoming environment for your game, in which each of
     the players can feel comfortable enough to dive into their
     roles and help entertain the whole crew.
         To that end, make sure to review the “Play It Safe” section in
     the first chapter. This includes the details on being considerate
     of the other players and taking the time to set up a Session
     Zero to help you anticipate any issues that might arise.
     FINDING PLAYERS
     The first thing to do aer reading this book is to find a group
     of people to play the game with. This can be its own challenge.
         If you have a group of friends you’re already playing
     games with, you can see if they’d like to take a crack at this
     game. They might know all about role-playing games and
     be eager to try something new, even just as a break from
     your standard fare.
         If you don’t have a ready-made group to play with, you
     can look for one locally. Gaming and comic-book conventions
     are a good way to meet like-minded folks. Or you can
     look online too.
         With the advent of teleconferencing soware and the
     rise of virtual tabletops, you don’t even have to be in the
     same country with people to play. It might make it easier
     if you’re in nearby time zones, but even being on the other
     side of the planet isn’t always a deal breaker.

     In Person
     If you’re running the game at home, make sure you have
     a good place to run the game and enough time set aside to
     play it. Many groups play games around dining or conference
     tables, but it’s entirely up to you.
          Running a game in the theater of the mind requires
     less preparation, and you can play it just about anywhere.
     However, many players enjoy using a map and miniatures to
     show exactly where the characters are at important moments.
     This requires a bit more time and effort to set up, but it helps
     bring the game alive, as the players can instantly see all
     their tactical options.
         You only need three six-sided (standard cubical) dice to
     play the game, but it’s even better if each player has their
     own set. Remember, one of the dice in each set should be
     different so you can instantly identify it as the Marvel die.
     It never hurts to have extra sets on hand just in case more
     people come to play or one of the dice goes rolling off.

                    Online
                    If you prefer to run your game online, it oen doesn’t require
                    as much preparation, as you can offload some of that to
                    the virtual tabletop of your choice. See Marvel.com/rpg for
                    officially licensed options that come ready to go. These come

                    easier to look up a rule with a search function rather than
                    flipping through the pages of a book.
                    RUNNING THE GAME
                    Once you have your players and their characters together and
                    you have an adventure ready for them to play, you should
                    be good to go. In the course of running the game, though,
                    you may run into a few tricky situations that aren’t fully
                    explained earlier in the rulebook.
                       That’s mostly because these are the sorts of things that
                    players don’t need to worry much about—or that Narrators
                    need to focus on more. Sometimes that’s because the issues
                    don’t come up that oen or at least not in every game. Other
                    times, it’s because such rules and tools are meant only for
                    the Narrator’s use.
                    When to Start Combat
                    The game can roll along just fine for an entire session without
                    any fights breaking out. If the players are having a good
                    time working that way, let them. For many heroes, combat
                    is the last resort.
                        In many cases, you should give the heroes a chance to
                    avoid combat. Maybe they can talk things out. Or they could
                    just dash around violent villains to save people directly. Not
                    everything has to wind up with people punching each other.
                        Of course, some players like the punching, so let them
                    lean into it if they like. Maybe the villains are the ones who
                    are trying to avoid fighting, then. Or maybe they’re ready
                    to throw down too.
                        To switch things up, you can also have the villains ambush
                    the heroes out of nowhere. That way, there are only two
                    options: fight or run.
                    Handling Initiative
                    Fights officially start when the Narrator says, “Roll for
                    initiative.” Everyone rolls a d616 and adds their Initiative
                    Modifier to their result.
                        That’s all pretty straightforward, but it can be a challenge
                    to keep track of the combat order, so take some time to
                    get it right before you start. That pays off all the way
                    through the fight.
                        The simplest way is to make two columns on a sheet
                    of paper. List the characters in order by their initiative
                    total—from highest to lowest—on the right, and write their
                    initiative check result next to each of them on the le.
                        If anyone gets a Fantastic success, put a star next to their
                    result. They get to take part in the bonus round before the
                    rest of the combat starts.
                        Then you start at the top of the order and work your way
                    down to the bottom. When you reach there, that’s the end
                    of the round.
                        It gets trickier if you have to control lots of opponents.
                    The best way to handle this is to see if you can group any of
Michael Syrett (Order #53194700)
      them together. Be sure to make initiative checks for major
      villains separately, though. They deserve their moment in
      the spotlight.
      Example: Daredevil, Iron Fist and Luke Cage are fighting Kingpin
      and Bullseye, along with five of Kingpin’s goons and four Hand
      ninja. Rather than making eleven different initiative checks, the
      Narrator can make four: one for Kingpin, one for Bullseye, one for
      the five goons and one for the four ninja. The various initiative
      checks come up:
         ◆ 16: Daredevil
         ◆ 15: Bullseye
         ◆ 14: Iron Fist, Luke Cage
         ◆ 12: Four Hand ninja
         ◆ 10: Kingpin
         ◆ 8: Five goons
          Daredevil goes first, and then Bullseye. Iron Fist and Luke Cage
      have the same number, but Iron Fist has the higher Vigilance, so
      he goes first. Then the Hand ninja go. Kingpin decides to hold his
      action until a©er his five goons act. Then he goes last.
      Picking Opponents
      In the middle of a battle, the Narrator oen has to pick who the
      various enemies are going to attack. When doing this, try to be
      fair and make sure that the enemies are choosing appropriate
      heroes to attack rather than all ganging up on a single hero
      at a time—unless they have a good reason to do that.
          Most opponents prefer to attack the hero they see as the
      biggest threat, either to their plans or to themselves. If a hero
      attacks a foe, the foe oen attacks back against that hero, if
      only out of self-defense. If a number of heroes have attacked
      the villain, the foe generally retaliates against whichever
      one of their attackers seems like the most dangerous. If they
      don’t know the heroes, they usually pick the one who has
      harmed them the most so far.
          It oen helps to explain your reasoning out loud so
      that the players understand why a particular character is
      being targeted.
          Remember, though, that villains have their own story,
      their own agendas and their own ways of doing things. If
      Doctor Octopus spots Spider-Man in the middle of a battle,
      for instance, he is sure to bypass as many other targets as
      he can so he can finally get his tentacles wrapped around
      the wall-crawler who has frustrated him for so long.
          In a similar vein, Kingpin doesn’t like to get his hands
      dirty when he can get someone else to do it for him. Given a
      choice, he prefers to call in his minions to do the dirty work,
      only stepping in once he is forced to.
          If you’re not sure which heroes a particular foe should
      attack, try to pare it down to the ones that are most eligible.
      Maybe they’re the closest ones, or maybe they seem
      equally dangerous.
          Then roll a single die to randomly choose one of the heroes
      as the foe’s target. If you have to decide between two targets,
                                                                             /10/ NARRATOR
      for instance, declare one of them to be picked on 1–3 and the
      other on 4–6, and then roll the die. If there are three possible
      targets, break it down to 1–2, 3–4 and 5–6.
          Once the opponents start pairing up, it’s okay to spread the
      fight around a bit. If a foe sees that one of their compatriots
      is already attacking a hero, that’s a good reason for them to
      attack a different hero instead.

                 Spreading Damage
                 Some powers and weapons spread their damage among
                 multiple targets. When that happens, make the attack roll
                 and figure damage normally. If the targets all have the
                 same amount of damage reduction, apply it and then split
                 the damage among them. If they have different amounts
                 of damage reduction, you need to figure the damage for
                 each character individually and then divide it by the same
                 number as usual aer that.
                TAKING BREAKS
                 While the game can be riveting fun, it’s impossible to keep
                 everyone on the edge of their seats for an entire session. A
                 good Narrator knows the worth of taking regular breaks
                 during a session.
                    When you do so, look around the table and ask, “Would
                 anyone like to take a break?” This isn’t a vote but a
                 survey. If anyone looks like they need a break—including
                 you—take one.
                    When you come back to the table to play, you’ll all be
                 better for it.
                Timing Breaks
                 A good rule of thumb is that you should take a break at least
                 every two hours, but if you know your players need them
                 more oen, don’t hesitate to have one as oen as once an hour.
                 You can set an alarm if you like, but it’s usually enough to
                 just keep your eye on the clock.
                     Every time the top of the hour comes around, consider
                 whether or not it’s a good time for a break. You don’t have
                 to announce this exactly on the hour, of course. Look for an
                 appropriate time to call a halt and then do it.
                 Breaking Points
                 If you can manage it, it’s good to call for a break right before
                 or aer a big moment in the game. That can be something like
                 a massive battle, a climactic confrontation with the villain
                 or a gigantic reveal of important information.
                     If you have the break before the big moment, that can
                 help people be ready to concentrate on it when it happens.
                 You don’t have to tell the players that something’s going to
                 happen, but they might guess at it.
                     It also gives you some extra time to prepare for the
                 moment. If you’re preparing for a combat, for instance, this
                 would be a great time to break out your battlemat and figures
                 if you have them. You can get everything ready to go then
                 without having the players sit there and wait for you to
                 set things up.
                     If you call for a break right aer a big moment, that gives
                 the players the chance to absorb whatever just happened.
                 They can discuss what their next moves might be, or they
                 can just clear their minds for a moment so they can come
                 back to the game fresh.
                     Again, if it’s aer a battle, this gives you a chance to clear
                 the table, assess the situation and see where you might want
                 to take the game next.
                     Either way, this keeps you from having to call a break in
                 the middle of that big moment. Interruptions can rob that
                 moment of its gravity. Ideally, you shouldn’t call a break in
                 the middle of combat—for instance—as players can lose
                 track of what’s happening over the course of time.
                                                         Art by Mike McKone, Andy Lann
Michael Syrett (Order #53194700)
        Agree on a Limit
        When you call for a break, set a limit on the break and
        announce the time when you want to resume the game. You
        can poll your players on this as well, but a good default is
        five minutes. You want to give people enough time to get a
        drink or a snack, go to the restroom, check their messages
        or whatever else they need to do—but not enough time to
        wander off and lose the game’s thread entirely.
            Tell the players how much time they have and then
        check the time and do the math. Tell them when you’d like
        to start up again.
            There are always exceptions to every rule, of course. This
        is not a film or a play that will start without people if they
        get delayed. You just want people to know when they’re
        expected to be ready to play again.
        To Be Continued
        When you sit down to play a session, you should also have
        at least a rough idea when the session is going to end. Be
        sure to communicate that expectation to the players, be it
        one hour, four hours or all day long. Sometimes the answer
        is, “Until something interrupts us,” which is fine too as long
        as everyone agrees to it.
             Ending a session is different than taking a break. You’re
        not just going to start back up in a few minutes. You might
        not play again for days or even weeks.
             If you haven’t finished the adventure you’re running—no
        matter its scope—it’s best to end a session on a moment that
        players will remember well and to give them something to be
        eager to return to. They should feel like they’ve accomplished
        something but that there’s still more ahead of them.
             If you can manage it, try not to end the session right
        before a big moment. Instead, it’s oen better to end aer
        a big moment and leave the question open about what the
        heroes might do next. That gives the players something to
        ponder between the sessions.
             If you can’t help ending before a big moment, try to run
        right up to it and leave it on a cliff-hanger. This can make
        the players eager to get back to the game to see what
        happens next.
        The Wrap-Up
        If you manage to complete a whole
        adventure by the end of your
        session, congratulations! Getting
        through a whole adventure is
        a triumph, and hopefully, you
        and the rest of the players had a
        wonderful time with it.
            This is a great time to ask
        people for feedback on how the
        game went for them. Every group
        of players is different, and you
        should do what you can to tailor
        the game to what works best for
        them and their tastes.

                       When asking players for feedback, be sure not to concentrate
                    only on things that they didn’t like. While that can be a good
                    place to start on making your sessions better, it’s just as
                    important to know about the things they enjoyed too. Otherwise,
                    you run the risk of eliminating those bits by design or neglect.
                    Advancement
                    Aer an adventure is over, that’s the perfect time to think
                    about character advancement—if you’re playing with
                    original characters or ones who have yet to hit their rank
                    cap. Before the game ends, let the players know if their
                    characters have gone up a rank. That can help wrap the
                    session up on a triumphant note.
                        That also gives the players something to do with their
                    characters until the next session. While you’re getting things
                    ready for the game, they can make the necessary additions
                    to their character sheet and pick out any new powers that
                    the increase in rank might allow them.
                        See the “Working With Ranks" section later in this chapter
                    for more details on this.
                    SCOPE
                    Running a Marvel Multiverse Role-Playing Game adventure
                    can be easy and fun. Before you start, though, you should
                    consider the scope of the game you want to run.
                       There are three different levels of scope—the expected
                    depth and length of a game—and it’s best to think of them in
                    terms of comic books. They are single issues, graphic novels
                    and ongoing series.
                    Single Issues
                    A single issue is a one-shot adventure. This is the kind of story
                    that would take place all within a single issue of a comic book.
                        As a game, you can expect it to last anywhere from two
                    to four hours or perhaps a bit longer. This is something you
                    plan to run in a single session. You might take a few breaks
                    in the middle, but you should be able to complete it in an
                    evening of play.
                        This is a great scope to work with if you’re playing the
                    game at a convention or as a way to try out the game. It
                    doesn’t require much of a commitment from anyone, and
                    it focuses on the fun in the immediate story rather than
                    teasing out threads for future adventures.
                        If players want to create their own characters for a single-
                    issue game, they can, but it’s much easier for the Narrator to
                    provide them each with a profile for an existing character
                    instead. In such games, the players don’t have as much time
                    to spend exploring their created characters and what they
                    might do in any given situation. It’s simpler just to jump in
                    and play one of their favorite Marvel super heroes instead.
                        As the Narrator, you can provide the players with a
                    selection of character sheets already filled in and ready to
                    go. If you can manage it, you can ask the players who their
                    preferred characters are beforehand, but you can also just
                    show up with a stack of ready-made character sheets and ask
                    the players to decide among themselves which characters
                    they’re each going to play.
                        The best thing about a single-issue game is that when
                    you’re done, you’re done. There’s no commitment to play
                    any longer. The story’s over.
                        Of course, there are always more stories to tell…
                                                                                        2
Michael Syrett (Order #53194700)
     Graphic Novels
     A graphic novel can be a longer, standalone story, or it can
     be a collection of single issues threaded together with an
     overarching plot or theme: a collected miniseries. You can
     start out with the plot of a full standalone story in mind, or
     you can use a single issue as a launchpad for developing the
     rest of the story. Either way is fine.
        With a graphic novel, you decide that the adventure is
     going to take a certain number of sessions, aer which you
     have a satisfying ending and are done. This can be anywhere
     from two sessions to five or more. Sometimes it’s hard to tell
     how many sessions such an adventure might take ahead of
     time, but don’t worry. The important part is that you, as the
     Narrator, know roughly how you plan for it to start and end.
        For examples of this, think of just about any Marvel comics
     trade paperback. Some of these are collected miniseries.
     Others are collected story arcs that take place as part of
     the backdrop of the ongoing series. Still others are original
     graphic novels created for that exact format.
        No matter how it comes about, when you’re done with
     a graphic novel, you and the rest of the players can feel a
     sense of accomplishment and triumph at having taken on
     and completed an epic story. That gives a good stopping
     place to step back and reassess how the game is going. Do
     you want to try another graphic novel? Would you rather
     try a single-issue adventure instead? Or maybe it’s time to
     consider continuing on with no set end in sight.
     Ongoing Series
     An ongoing series of adventures is much like an ongoing
     comic-book series. It’s a series of connected adventures—
     some single-issue ones and some graphic-novel ones—
     featuring a group of characters. The stories told in the
     course of the series can vary wildly in length, and there
     may be several overarching plots that thread themselves
     throughout the series.
         Some of these plot threads can propel the characters
     on through an untold number of adventures without fully
     resolving. Others might wrap up much more quickly. Either
     way, when one plot or story wraps up, another one begins.
     This can go on for untold years.
         While that might sound like a huge commitment, there’s
     no need to let that get in your way. If you break the series
     down into smaller, more manageable sections, that gives the
     players—including the Narrator—a chance to achieve a sense
     of satisfaction and even closure on a regular basis without
     cutting them off from the promise of future adventures.
         For a Narrator, running an ongoing series can be a huge
     challenge, but you don’t need to commit to it all at once. You
     can start out with a single issue or two and see how they go.
     If that works, you can move up to graphic novels. Aer a
     couple of those go well, you can string them all together to
     form the basis of an ongoing series.
         You don’t need to tell people what you have planned. You
                                                                       /10/ NARRATOR
     don’t even need to decide that for yourself. You just need to
     jump in and play and see where the game and your fellow
     players take you.
     ILLUSIONS & MIRAGES
     Some characters can cast illusions or create mirages designed
     to fool others into thinking that they are real. In game terms,
81
===PDFPAGE 283===
                  /10/ NARRATOR
                 an illusion is an image—sometimes with accompanying
                 sound or other sensations—of something that isn’t actually
                 there. The person creating it doesn’t have to make an action
                 check to activate it. Instead, others must make a Logic check
                 against the creator’s Ego defense.
                    A mirage works similarly to an illusion, but the false
                 imagery isn’t created for people to observe. Instead, it’s
                 created directly in the minds of the people affected by it.
                 The observers still make a Logic check to see if they can
                 determine that the mirage is fake. Instead of making it
                 against the creator’s Ego defense, though, they make it
                 against their Logic defense.
                 Convincing Imagery
                 If imagery generated by an illusion or mirage is particularly
                 convincing—if it depicts something that the viewer might
                 expect to see—the viewer should have trouble with their
                 Logic check to see through the deception. For instance, if
                 the imagery looks like a bus rolling through a school zone
                 at a low speed, a reasonable viewer might expect to see
                 something like that. Even if the imagery is covering up the
                 heroes who are jogging along inside of it.
                     If the imagery is of something a viewer is unlikely to
                 accept at face value, then they should get an edge on their
                 Logic check to see through it. If they turn a corner and see
                 themselves standing there, for instance, they are probably not
                 going to believe it and would immediately start wondering
                 what kind of trick was being played on them.
                     Some characters—like Mysterio—who rely heavily on
                 imagery have been known to combine it with practical effects
                 and disguises. This can help keep a target guessing about
                 what’s real and what’s not, even when they know that there’s
                 someone manipulating imagery around them.
                 Overlapping Imagery
                 Most of the time, a bit of imagery generated by a power is
                 pretty straightforward. The character creates it, and those
                 around them attempt to see through it. Sometimes things
                 get a bit more complicated.
                     If the imagery is attempting to cover up something
                 real—rather than simply existing in an empty space, for
                 instance—the creator must take special care. Otherwise,
                 observers should be suspicious. This isn’t so much a matter
                 of giving an observer an edge on their Logic check, although
                 that can happen. It’s more about making sure that observers
                 don’t have a reason to take a closer look at the imagery. An
                 image of a solid wall that people keep moving through, for
                 instance, should garner some attention.
                     It can get even trickier if more than one person attempts
                 to generate imagery in the same place. If it is possible for
                 them to coexist logically, then everything works normally,
                 but if the imageries conflict, then only one of them should
                 continue to exist.
                     If an illusion and a mirage conflict, the mirage takes
                 precedence. It affects not the light going into the eyes but
                 how the mind interprets them.
                     If the conflicting imagery springs all from illusions or all
                 from mirages, the characters generating the imagery must
                 make an action check using either Ego (for illusions) or Logic
                 (for mirages). The imagery of the character with the highest
                 result takes precedence over any others.
Michael Syrett (Order #53194700)
          If the other imagery isn’t entirely covered up or blocked
      by the winning imagery, though, this can make observers
      suspicious. They should have an edge on any Logic checks
      to see through any of the involved imagery.
      MIND CONTROL
      Some powers allow characters to control or influence another
      person’s mind. These can be fraught with all sorts of danger
      and not just inside the game. Before such powers are used
      in your game—whether by the Narrator’s characters or any
      of the players’ characters—you should have a conversation
      with your players about what they feel comfortable with.
          Taking control of another person’s mind is a violation of
      their agency, and this can be deeply disturbing depending
      on the degree. It’s one thing to order someone to ignore
      something or to walk away, and another entirely to force
      them to commit acts they would never otherwise consider. It
      doesn’t matter much to the controlled person if the controller
      thinks they’re doing it for a good reason or not.
          This discussion can be part of your Session Zero chat, but
      it might not come up until later. If it does, then you should
      open the discussion again.
          If you do decide to allow such powers in the game, you
      should explore the many available safety tools for your
      game. While discussing the matter ahead of time, players
      might not think that a loss of control over their character—or
      watching it happen to someone else—would bother them,
      but they could change their mind in the middle of a session
      once it actually happens.
      Lost Memories
      Outside of direct mind control, there are also powers that
      allow a character to erase, amend or edit the memories of
      other people. This can prove disturbing to players as well,
      as it implies that the affected characters either did things or
      had things done to them that they can’t remember.
          In some cases, this can be an excellent mystery around
      which you can base an adventure. What happened? Why can’t
      the characters remember? Who did this to them?
          But it can also be more than some people care to explore.
      There can be a fine line between an intriguing mystery and
      a traumatic incident. It’s better to ask them about this sort
      of thing ahead of time rather than springing it on them.
      OMNIVERSAL TRAVEL
      The Ominiversal Travel power set is rife with opportunities
      for trouble and abuse. Used well and properly, these powers
      can open up many avenues of adventure for the game. Used
      poorly, they can total up to a lot of headaches.
          It’s best to establish some ground rules for these powers,
      depending on how you and your players want to use them.
      Just remember that rules for the players’ characters should
      also extend to the rest of the characters in the game.
          Here are some suggestions for how to handle these powers.
      You are, of course, free to use them as you like. Just know
      that they hold the potential to gravely disrupt the regular
      flow of the game.
      Multiversal/Dimensional Travel
      These powers are meant to allow the character to travel to
      other dimensions or universes and back. They shouldn’t be

                    used to bring other characters in—or at least not without a
                    great deal of preparation ahead of time.
                        A character shouldn’t generally be able to, for instance,
                    reach into a Multiverse, tap an alternate version of
                    themselves—or anyone else, for that matter—on their
                    shoulder, and bring them into the middle of a combat. For
                    one, most people aren’t ready and willing to fight someplace
                    else without any kind of warning or preparation.
                        Just in terms of timing, this would be difficult if not
                    impossible to manage. Each round only lasts about 5 seconds.
                    If someone the character is trying to summon says, “Just give
                    me a minute,” a full 12 rounds would pass in that minute.
                    The battle would likely be over by the time they managed
                    to get ready and join it.
                        Such powers should instead be used to travel at less
                    fraught moments, not to jump back and forth in an attempt
                    to influence the outcome of a battle. Traveling to different
                    dimensions or universes is not something that should be
                    undertaken lightly, as it’s not always guaranteed that the
                    travelers can make it back home—or that their home will
                    be the same as they remember it if they’re able to return.
                        When a character moves back and forth between such
                    places, they should have a plan in place. Just jumping around
                    between dimensions and universes can attract the wrong
                    kind of attention.
                        If a character is desperate, they should be able to use their
                    power to escape from a bad situation, even in the middle of
                    a fight. That allows them to leave the battle, possibly saving
Michael Syrett (Order #53194700)
       their life or the lives of others they care about. However,
       that generally removes them completely from the combat.
           You can make exceptions for this if you like, but this is
       something that should be discussed with the players so they
       know what’s expected and considered fair.
           For example, a character might set up a safe house or an
       armory or a supply station in another dimension or realm
       that they can get to whenever they need to. They can use
       their power to access it on one action, take another action
       to grab the things they need and then take a third action
       to return to the fight. That takes them out of the battle for a
       good period of time, but that’s the price they pay for having
       access to what they want when they need it.
           Of course, someone else could find their cache or safe
       house while they’re not around and strip it to the walls. It
       might not have what they want when they really need it. Or
       there might be someone waiting there for them.
       Time Travel
       Traveling through time opens up all sorts of potential
       problems. Be sure to note that there’s a rule against going
       back into a particular round in a battle to change things.
                                                                         /10/ NARRATOR
       That’s less because it couldn’t be technically possible—it
       could be—and more because it would require a horrendous
       amount of bookkeeping to keep track of every battle the
       characters are in due to the possibility that they might want
       to go back and change things at some point.
           That’s also because no one likes to feel like everything
       they’ve accomplished in a game is wasted. If the character

                  //10/

                 does it over and over again until the dice happen to turn up
                 in their favor, it quickly becomes tiresome.
                     If just as a battle is going to end, a character travels back
                 to the first round in the game, what happens to the characters
                 they leave behind? Technically, they’re all stuck back in that
                 previous timeline, probably never to be seen again. From the
                 time-traveler’s point of view, though, they’re all right there,
                 just a hair younger than before. The same thing happens if
                 the character starts going back into the recent past outside
                 of battle as well.
                     If a character goes back into the recent past without
                 their teammates, have the other players take over playing
                 their same characters, just as if nothing had happened. The
                 trouble is that they must play as if they don’t have any of
                 the knowledge of what’s happened in the time-traveler’s
                 timeline, and as the Narrator, you may be obliged to remind
                 them about this.
                     If a character travels through time to meet themselves
                 in the past or the future, they should continue controlling
                 the time-traveling character. As the Narrator, you should
                 control their other self, who may not react in the way that
                 the time-traveling character might hope. If it’s in the past,
                 maybe the character is disturbed to see their future self and
                 begins worrying incessantly about the future.
                     If it’s in the future, the character might not appreciate the
                 interruption from their past self. Things may have happened
                 to them that the past self might find disturbing too. They
                 might even travel back in time to stop the character from
                 interfering with them.
                     The safest way to travel in time is for the travelers to
                 make sure that they go far enough in either direction to
                 ensure that they’re not going to wind up interfering with
                 their own history or fate.
                 Interventions
                 If a character abuses their time-travel powers too much,
                 they can expect to receive a visit from someone invested
                 in keeping people from making massive alterations to the
                 timeline. Call it an intervention. This could be from Kang,
                 Immortus, Doctor Doom or any number of other powerful
                 people. They have their own plans for the timeline, aer all,
                 and they frown—sometimes brutally—on those who might
                 spoil their efforts.
                     Or it could be from the Time Variance Authority. This
                 is a massive (theoretically infinite) bureaucracy of time-
                 traveling agents who have been put in charge of making
Michael Syrett (Order #53194700)
      sure that nothing happens to the countless timelines that
      they are in charge of. That includes correcting issues caused
      by time-traveling characters who indiscriminately alter
      the course of time.
          The TVA operates out of the Null-Time Zone, an overarching
      dimension that exists outside of the natural flow of time.
      From there, TVA agents can travel to various points of time
      in any of the universes that they oversee.
          Depending on the circumstances, TVA agents oen let
      first-time offenders who have risen to the point of warranting
      their attention off with a warning. This might come in the
      form of a note that proves its provenance by telling the reader
      something that will happen to them in the next few minutes.
          If necessary, the TVA has been known to capture repeat
      offenders and hold them in time cells in which they are
      trapped in an infinitely repeating loop of time until they
      are brought before the Time Courts to have their case heard.
      However, the TVA prefers to find solutions in which the order
      of time is preserved. This oen includes having the offender
      help them repair any continuity errors caused by time travel
      or resolve any perceived time paradoxes that sprang from
      their injudicious time travel.
          Because of the nature of time in the Marvel Multiverse,
      time paradoxes don’t actually exist. They just cause a new
      universe to be started that branches off from the time at
      which the paradox happened. However, repairing such
      differences can cause the timestreams of the perhaps-split
      universes to merge again, making them essentially the same
      universe once more.
      SOCIAL INTERACTIONS
      Conversations and other social interactions with other
      characters happen a lot in a game. Oen you don’t need to
      use any dice or rules to help you decide how such things
      progress. You can just use your best judgment.
         If Mister Fantastic asks someone on the street for
      directions, for instance, most people would be happy to
      lend a hand. He’s world-famous and known to be one of the
      greatest heroes on the planet. Pointing him in the right
      direction is the least they can do.
         If Wolverine (Logan)—in full costume and with claws
      popped—snarls at someone to get out of the way, only the
      grumpiest or most stubborn people are going to stand their
      ground against him. His reputation as a no-nonsense brawler
      precedes him.
284
===PDFPAGE 286===
                        However, if Wolverine snarls at Sabretooth to get out of
                    the way, that’s just not going to fly. The two have a history
                    that goes back decades, and it regularly ends in violence.
                        But sometimes, things aren’t so clear-cut. If Wolverine
                    snarls at a Hydra agent to run, what’s going to happen? Will
                    the Hydra agent stand their ground and shoot at the hero, or
                    will they tuck their tail between their legs and flee?
                        That’s when it’s time to have Wolverine’s player break
                    out their dice and make an action check.
                        When a character is trying to address someone’s feelings—
                    whether fear, love, ambition, responsibility or whatever—
                    that calls for an Ego check. If the character is attempting
                    to convince someone of something by use of facts and
                    knowledge—as would happen in a laboratory, a court of
                    law or many other venues—that calls for a Logic check.
                        The target number for such a check is the target’s Ego or
                    Logic defense. The higher the defense, the more resistant
                    the target is to being influenced in such a way.
                        Feel free to adjust the target number up or down
                    depending on how well the character’s player role-plays their
                    part. You can also give the character trouble or an edge for
                    things like the target’s fear of reprisals or other consequences
                    from other people. Someone guarding a door, for instance, is
                    unlikely to give into any but the most determined threats, as
                    they know other people are depending on them, and that if
                    they just walk away, they are likely going to be out of a job.
                        On a success, the target hesitates, willing to consider the
                    character’s request (or demand) and to give them another
                    chance at convincing them. The character then gets an edge
                    on a subsequent attempt along the same lines.
                        On a Fantastic success, the target caves instantly.
                        Just because the target gives into a character, though,
                    doesn’t mean that the two of them are now besties for
                    life. It simply means that the target decided to acquiesce
                    to the character—for now. That can change in an instant,
                    especially if someone with a stronger influence on the target
                    can reach them.
                    Example: Wolverine storms into a building and spots a Hydra
                    agent on the other side of the room. He knows he can’t get to the
                    agent to attack them this turn. Instead, he charges toward the
                    agent at full speed and growls out, “You oughta find another line
                    of work, bub. Fast!”
                        The Narrator sees this as an intimidation attempt against
                    the Hydra agent’s Ego defense of 11. Wolverine only has an Ego
                    of 1 himself, but because of his claws and the player’s excellent
                    demeanor, the Narrator gives Wolverine an edge on the action
                    check. The player rolls and gets 2 3 4, plus his Ego of 1, for a total
                    of 10, not quite enough. The player uses their edge to reroll their
                    Marvel die and gets a 6. That brings the total to 13, which is plenty.
                        The Narrator decides that the Hydra agent loses their action to
                    tremble in fear and say, “Whoa, hey now! Hold on just a minute!”
                        The next turn, Wolverine’s player decides that he likes how
                    this is going for him. Wolverine stalks up to the Hydra agent,
                    scraping his claws against each other as he goes. “Weren’t you
                    listening to me, bub? Last chance.”
                        Wolverine makes another Ego check with an edge. This time
                    he rolls 2 M 4, which is a Fantastic success! The Hydra agent turns
                    and bolts in the opposite direction, screaming the whole way.

      Heroes and Villains
      Note that players don’t generally have to make action checks
      for how their character behaves unless someone is using
      some kind of power against them. You should assume the
      player has full control over the character and can make their
      own decisions about how their character responds and acts.
          The same goes for major villains. It’s one thing to face
      down a Rank 1 hireling, but someone like the Red Skull
      isn’t going to back down so easily. If there’s a question in
      your mind about how a major villain would react to such
      manipulation attempts, feel free to have the hero make an
      action check, but interpret the results with the villain’s full
      motivations and history with the character in mind.
      CREATING NEW POWERS
      While this book features hundreds of powers—enough
      for you to be able to design all sorts of different kinds of
      characters with—it cannot cover every potential power
      that has appeared in Marvel comics, much less every power
      that players might wish to have available for their original
      creations. We may add more powers in future books as needed,
      but in the meantime, there’s no reason you can’t create your
      own unofficial versions for use in your game.
         We recommend that players stick to the published powers
      to start with, but once you have the hang of how those
      work in the game, you should be ready to take a crack at
      making up your own.
      Rifﬁng Powers
      Before you go too far along the path of creating whole new
      powers, though, take a look at the existing powers and see
      if you can simply adapt them to your own needs. Many of
      them are meant to be generic enough that they can at least
      form the basis for all kinds of powers.
          For example, if you want to have powers that resemble the
      Elemental Control power set but have a different basis than
      the ones listed, you could just add a new style to those powers
      and perhaps come up with a new special effect. Maybe you
      want a Darkness element, for instance, although the special
      effect for that would likely be that it blinds the target for
      one round, much like the Energy element does.
          That’s absolutely fine! Even if the power set works the
      same as another power set and the difference is really only
      in tone, tone still matters.
          Not every part of a character can be defined by their
      powers. A lot of their story and the way they interact with
      others—and are seen by others—comes down to the tone
      that they and their powers create.
      Substitute Powers
      You might also find the powers you want from power sets
      you wouldn’t expect. Invisibility powers, for instance, come
      under the Illusion power set because they’re all about fooling
      an observer’s perceptions.
                                                                        /10/ NARRATOR
          The Invisible Woman, though, only takes the invisibility
      powers from that set. For her force-field powers, she turns
      to the Elemental Control set instead, using the Force style.
      There’s no single power set that describes the entirety of
      her powers, so she blends a couple different ones to come
      up with what she needs.
          Turn to Chapter 8 for countless similar examples.

                 Power Sets
                 The first thing to consider is whether you want to work up
                 an entire power set or just a single power. Either is fine,
                 although coming up with a whole set can be a bit more work.
                 The smallest power sets at the moment have no fewer than
                 5 powers, while the largest ones have dozens.
                    The first thing to think of with a power set is the theme
                 that it’s wrapped around. Make sure that you can’t fi nd
                 anything similar to it in the existing powers and power sets.
                 Don’t forget to take a close look at the basic powers. Some of
                 these were made into basic powers because they fit so well
                 with so many other power sets that it made more sense to
                 just make them freely available to anyone without hitching
                 them to a particular power set.
                     Once you have an idea for the power set, think about
                 the various ways in which a character can use that power.
                 Some of these are bound to be more potent than others, and
                 some of them also naturally lead from one power to another.
                    A character can’t have, for instance, Hurled Shield Bash
                 before they take the Shield Bash power. Having one without
                 the other wouldn’t make much sense. Similarly, they can’t
                 take the Rico-Shield power until they have the Hurled Shield
                 Bash power. You can’t bounce a shield expertly off your foes
                 before you know how to throw it at them first, aer all.
                    Think about the various things you’d like to see the
                 character do with the power set and then build the powers
                 around that. If you’re trying to model them on an existing
                 character, this might be a bit easier, as you hopefully then
                 have lots of examples to draw upon. If you’re coming up with
                 something original, then you might need to plumb a little
                 deeper into your imagination to make it all gel together.
                     Once you have a broad outline of various entries in your
                 power set ready to go, then it’s time to delve into creating
                 the actual powers.
                 Powers
                 You should model the power you’re creating on the powers
                 in this book. That means thinking about the various entries
                 in a standard power description and how you would fi ll
                 them in. These are:
                     ▶ Power Set: You don’t need to build an entire power
                          set, but if you do, you should list it here. If there’s no
                          power set, then it’s a basic power by default.
                     ▶ Prerequisites: A list of any powers, traits, rank and
                          so on that the character must have to use this power.
                          More powerful powers tend to have more prerequisites.
                     ▶ Action: Standard, movement or reaction. If this is
                          something a character uses during movement, then
                          it’s a movement action. If they might use it in an instant
                          to save themselves or someone else, then it’s probably
                          a reaction power. Otherwise, it likely uses a standard
                          action. Or maybe some combination of the three.
                     ▶ Trigger: If this power uses a reaction, this is where
                          you describe what could trigger the reaction. You
                          can be as specific as you like, but the more generic it
                          is, the more oen it can be used.
                     ▶ Duration: Is it a permanent power (at least
                          once activated)? Is it over in an instant? Do its
                          effects last for just a single round? Does it require
                          concentration to keep active?
Michael Syrett (Order #53194700)
          ▶ Range: If the power is meant to be used at a
             distance, list a range here. Remember that the listed
             range is the maximum distance to use the power
             without trouble. From that point to double the
             listed range, the action has trouble. Beyond that, it
             can’t be done.
          ▶ Cost: If there’s a cost to the power (oen in Focus),
             it’s listed here. Note that the standard Focus cost
             for a power is its rank requirement (if any) minus
             1, multiplied by 5. For example, a power with a
             prerequisite of Rank 4 would cost ([4–1]×5=) 15
             Focus to use.
          ▶ Effect: What does the power do? Does it require an
             action check? If so, is there a target number for it or
             a descriptor like Challenging? Or is the check meant
             to be made against someone else’s defense score? If
             there’s an action check, what happens on a success?
             How about a Fantastic success?
           When coming up with all these details for your new power,
       use the existing powers as a model. If the power seems like it
       fits in well with the ones that are already published, you’re
       probably doing a good job with it.
       Unique Powers
       Sometimes there are powers that seem to defy description.
       As much as you might want to, you just can’t get them to fit
       inside the standard power description’s boxes.
            That’s all right. As long as you and everyone else in your
       game agree to use them the way you describe them, they
       should work just fine.
            If you can, be sure to run these powers past the other
       people in the game before you use them. Otherwise, they
       might not seem fair to the other players. In particular, the
       Narrator should sign off on any powers that another player
       comes up with.
            As the Narrator, though, you don’t always have to explain
       every aspect of the powers of one of the characters you’re
       controlling. If you say they can do something, then they do
       it. Just be careful not to abuse this, or the other players may
       get frustrated.
            Even if you can’t fit the powers a character is using into
       the game’s rules, the power should still have rules. Write
       down how it works, and be consistent about how you use
       it in the game. If things change without reason, the other
       players are likely to notice and wonder just what’s going on.
            For example, Isca the Unbeaten is an ancient mutant from
       Arakko, the island that was split off from Krakoa thousands
       of years ago. Her power is that she cannot lose. It doesn’t
       matter if it’s a fight, a foot race or a simple bet, she cannot
       lose—even if she wants to.
            This power doesn’t fit into the framework for powers in
       this book. It’s less of a set of powers and more of a narrative
       device—and that’s okay. It makes Isca powerful, but it also
       makes her tragic. She cannot lose a battle, but that means
       that she is sometimes forced to switch sides in a battle so
       that she is on the winning side.
            Playing Isca would be tricky, and it’s not a challenge that
       inexperienced players should try to take on. But it can make
       for some amazing stories in the hands of a great player—or
       a great Narrator.

                 Cosmos-Shaking Powers
                 Some characters and their powers are simply too powerful
                 to work within the current framework of the game. This
                 includes metaphorical entities like Eternity or Death. Their
                 powers have few if any limits, and they have little interest
                 in the sorts of conflicts that drive most adventures of the
                 kind that you find in Marvel comics.
                     As such, we recommend that players steer clear of trying
                 to play characters with such ineffable powers. The Narrator
                 should be able to use them with restraint, but such encounters
                 with the players’ characters should be rare.
                     If a character seems like they would be more powerful
                 than the Rank 6 characters listed in this book, they’re
                 probably too powerful for players to take on their role in
                 most games. It’s possible to make an intriguing and amazing
                 game with such cosmos-shaking characters, but that’s beyond
                 the scope of most Marvel comics stories—and of this book.
                 WORKING WITH RANKS
                 If you’re playing a game with existing Marvel characters,
                 you don’t have to worry about how the characters are going
                 to gain ranks. Aer their origin stories are complete, most
                 Marvel characters are already at the highest rank they can
                 be. Spider-Man (for instance) is never going to be as powerful
                 as Thor, no matter how many adventures he goes on.
                     If your game includes original characters created by
                 your players, though, they would probably like to know
                 how to increase their rank as they play the game. In general,
                 completing a graphic-novel–sized adventure—one that
                 lasts anywhere from four to six sessions—should allow a
                 character to go up one rank in the downtime between that
                 adventure and the next one. However, the speed at which
                 the characters advance is really up to both them and you.
                 Starting Ranks
                 Before you start your game, you should chat with your
                 players about what rank they want their characters to start
                 at. While it seems natural to start at Rank 1, there’s no reason
                 you can’t just as easily start at Rank 2, Rank 4 or any other
                 rank you like.
                      If you’re playing through a published adventure, it might
                 describe itself as being “For three to five heroes of Rank 3 to
                 4.” You could play other adventures until your players’ heroes
                 are ready for that challenge, but it’s also perfectly fine to
                 have them all start at Rank 3 instead. There’s no reason for
                 the players to have to grind through those earlier ranks just
                 so they can play in that adventure—unless they want to!
                 Rank Caps
                 The other conversation you should have is about what the
                 rank caps for the characters should be. If you’re planning on
                 running a campaign that sticks mostly to one neighborhood
                 in New York City, for instance, the characters shouldn’t
                 be above Rank 3. If they are, the challenges they face
                 there might be too easy for them. Thor doesn’t spend a
                 lot of time patrolling rooops for purse snatchers or bank
                 robbers, aer all.
                     A rank cap sets a goal for the kind of game that you and
                 your players want to play. If it’s about fighting local crime,
                 capping it at Rank 2 or Rank 3 is fine. If it’s about saving the
                 galaxy, a rank cap of 5 or even 6 might work better.
Michael Syrett (Order #53194700)
          If you decide you want to change your game’s rank cap
      at some point, that’s easy enough—as long as you’re liing
      it and not lowering it. If you want to lower it, make sure
      that the players all agree with the decision—and that none
      of their characters are already beyond that new rank cap.
      Few players like having to scale their characters down to a
      lower rank, as it feels like throwing their achievements away.
      Doing this as part of a temporary throwback or a flashback
      session could be fun, but a permanent loss might be too much.
          Raising the rank cap so the characters can test themselves
      against more powerful threats, though, can be exciting.
          Remember, the default rank cap for any character is 6. If
      you and the players don’t decide on a cap, that’s the highest
      their characters can go in any case.
      Gaining Ranks
      When a character goes up a rank, they gain the following things:
         ▶ +5 ability points
         ▶ +1 trait
         ▶ +4 powers
         ▶ +1 to their damage multipliers
         ▶ +1 Karma
         ▶ Plus, they may get bonuses to all sorts of secondary
            statistics based on the above increases
          That’s a large leap in effectiveness, and it changes the
      sorts of challenges they’re able to take on. Most characters can
      handle themselves against opponents of their own rank. Foes
      that are a rank above them are sure to be more challenging.
      If there’s a difference of two or more ranks between them,
      the challenge might be too much for them to overcome—
      although there are always extenuating circumstances that
      might be able to tip the balance in their favor.
      Mixing Ranks
      It’s easiest to play with a group of characters that are all at
      similar ranks. You don’t have to worry about the villains
      being too tough for some and too easy for others. The heroes
      can just mix and match foes as they prefer, as they’re all
      roughly of the same power level.
           However, there are lots of examples of super-hero teams
      that feature characters of differing ranks. The Avengers are
      such a team, for instance, and they work fantastically well
      together, even with street-level characters like Hawkeye
      fighting alongside mythical gods like Thor.
           To make this work in a game, it’s up to the Narrator to
      come up with challenges that are suitable for characters of
      varying ranks. Each player should have their moment in
      the spotlight to shine during each play session, and when
      you’re faced with a team of mixed ranks, that requires a
      much stronger hand with craing encounters.
           For example, if the Avengers are facing off against Thanos,
      the highest-rank heroes can try to take on the Titan toe-
      to-toe, but the lower-rank ones might not feel too useful.
      To counter that, you can pit the lower-rank heroes against
      some of Thanos’ subordinates, if only to keep such threats
      from bothering their more powerful friends. Or they can
      spend their time saving innocents endangered by Thanos’
      appearance. Or maybe they can use their special traits and
      powers to execute a complicated way to defeat Thanos while
288
===PDFPAGE 290===
                    their higher-ranked friends buy them the time they need
                    to put their plan into action.
                        Similarly, if the villain is of a low rank—suitable to the
                    lower-rank heroes on the team—you can present the team
                    with a larger threat that the villain has set up to draw
                    attention to something else. Maybe they’ve put bombs all
                    around the city. Or they’ve opened a gateway to a demonic
                    dimension. Or unleased a kaiju on the city. The high-rank
                    heroes can run off to deal with that threat while the other
                    heroes contend directly with the responsible villain to put
                    an end to their deeper plot.
                        You know your players and their heroes better than
                    anyone. No one can do a better job of tailoring such
                    challenges than you.
                    ADJUSTING ADVENTURES
                    Whether playing a published adventure or one of your own
                    creation, you might find that the adventure isn’t quite suited
                    to the characters taking part in the game. Sometimes the
                    adventure is too hard for the characters, which leads to
                    frustration. Other times it might prove too easy, which can
                    lead to boredom.
                        If either of these things happen, you can try to adjust
                    the difficulty of the adventure on the fly to improve
                    the experience.
                    Making It Fit
                    The fi rst thing to ask is whether the adventure and the
                    characters are a good fit. Adjusting the adventure’s challenge
                    is probably worth it if the characters are within a rank or
                    two of being suited for it. Moving things around to suit a
                    bigger difference might not be worth the bother.
                        If a character was made for patrolling the streets of
                    Brooklyn, then confronting the likes of Galactus might
                    be too much for them, no matter how high you crank up
                    everything available to them. Similarly, Thor is going to get
                    bored beating up purse snatchers, even if he’s lost Mjolnir
                    for a while.
                                                                                     2

Michael Syrett (Order #53194700)
         If the problem is that the characters aren’t ready for the
     adventure you’re planning, then it might be better to just
     wait until they are—assuming they haven’t already hit their
     rank cap and are still able to gain ranks. You can send them
     on all sorts of other adventures in which they can hone their
     skills, gain experience and learn more about themselves and
     their powers. You can move them into that more challenging
     adventure when they’re ready, and they would appreciate it
     even more, as it should feel like a natural progression for them.
         If, instead, the problem is that the characters are just too
     powerful to want to bother with the adventure, you might
     want to just skip it. The players clearly want to be tackling
     bigger issues, so there’s no need to make them walk through
     an adventure their characters might find trivial. You can still
     use that adventure you have in hand as an inspiration for
     bigger and more challenging stories that make for a better fit.
     Toning Things Down
     If you’re determined to play through an adventure that’s
     rated for a lower rank than the characters in your game,
     there are two simple options.
         First, you could have the players take on the roles of
     different characters for the adventure. Aer all, there’s no
     rule that says they have to play the same characters every
     time they sit down at the table. They’re more than welcome to
     create new characters who are a better fit for the adventure.
         If they’d rather not come up with whole new characters
     just for this adventure, that’s fine. You can provide them
     with appropriate profiles of Marvel heroes from this book
     instead. Just copy their details on to fresh character sheets
     for each player, and you’re all set.
         If your players don’t seem up for that, there’s a second
     option: the flashback. You can set the adventure at a date
     in the past during which the characters were of the rank
     that works best. Just tell the players what rank you need
     their characters to be and have them create trimmed-down
     versions of their characters.
         This can be an excellent chance to explore the histories
     of these characters that might not otherwise come up. You
     and the players can learn more about the characters and
     what drives them, and those revelations can affect their
             present-day adventures as well.
                 You could—if you like—play parallel games set
              in different times in the characters’ lives, moving
              back and forth among them as you like. Eventually,
              those lower-rank characters are fated to become the
                                     higher-rank characters, but
                                       they might take a long and
                                        convoluted path to get there.
                                              If the younger ones
                                           die, are maimed or
                                          otherwise substantially
                                       change so that the older
                         team is unlikely to ever happen, then the
                        younger characters’ supposed fate must have
                                                                         /10/ NARRATOR
                       been thwarted. You can either come up with
                     a way for the two sections of the timeline to
                    match up properly, or you can just declare that
     the two sets of characters are now in divergent timelines—
     which means alternate universes. This can present its own
     challenges, but it also means that the time is ripe for the two
     sets of characters to actually meet each other too.

                  /10/ NARRATOR
                 Cranking Things Up
                 You can do the same thing if the adventure calls for more
                 powerful characters than the players currently have. Flash
                 forward to set the game in a possible future for those heroes
                 and have the players develop versions of their characters
                 at the necessary rank. These don’t have to be the final form
                 those characters are fated to become. They could simply be
                 versions from a potential future. It’s all up to you and the
                 decisions the players make as their characters advance.
                     (You could also use the flash-forward to power the
                 characters down, as in the case of Old Man Logan and
                 many other Marvel heroes, but check with your players
                 first to see if they’re interested in playing their heroes
                 in their twilight years.)
                     If the players aren’t up for that, you can see if they
                 might want to play different heroes for this particular
                 adventure. It might be time for some bigger heroes to
                 step in and take care of things instead—under the
                 players’ control, of course.
                     One answer to this problem that comes straight from
                 the comics is for the characters to go out and find new
                 weapons or equipment—or even other characters—that
                 can help even the score for them. This kind of quest
                 to find such help can constitute a whole adventure
                 all by itself.
                     If you’re playing in a single-issue or graphic-novel
                 game, you can usually leave the character with their
                 extra help at the end of the adventure. The heroes
                 did what it took to line up the help they needed, and
                 they carried the day. The end.
                     If you’re playing in an ongoing series, though,
                 the characters shouldn’t get to keep all of those
                 things that they needed for this one adventure.
                 When everything’s said and done, they should
                 return to their regular life—including their
                 standard rank cap, assuming they’ve reached it.
                     Because of that, if you’re going to crank things
                 up for the characters with this kind of help, make
                 sure to let the players know that their characters
                 aren’t going to have permanent access to this
                 extra stuff and the help that it conveys. If you’re
                 clever, you can build an expiration date into the
                 help they are offered, so it feels natural when
                 that help disappears. For example, in Fear Itself
                 (2011), the heroes were able to create special
                 uru weapons to defeat Cul the Serpent and the
                 Worthy, but all that uru had to be returned to
                 the Asgardians once its purpose was served.
                 CHANGING HEROES
                 Aer every adventure is complete, it’s a
                 good idea to take a moment to look over the
                 character sheets with your players and see if
                 it’s time to make some changes. Just because
                 a character hit their rank cap doesn’t mean
                 they’re not capable of change. It just means
                 they’re not likely to get much more
                 powerful. There are still all sorts of
                 ways that their adventures can affect
                 them and the people around them.
