                    Changing Labels
                    The most obvious way for a character to change without
                    gaining rank is through their labels: their traits and their tags.
                        Tags are simple to change. There are no limits on how
                    many a character can have, and they can be added and
                    removed at will. For instance, if a character has the Secret
                    Identity tag but gets unmasked on the internet, it’s time to
                    drop that tag and pick up the Public Identity one instead.
                        The trick is to make sure that the players keep their
                    characters’ tags up to date.
                        The most important tag—and the one that deserves the
                    most attention—is Heroic. If a character isn’t acting in a
                    heroic way—in particular, if they attempt to kill someone—
                    then you should discuss removing the tag from the character.
                         Characters with the Heroic tag start out with fresh
                     Karma points every day, so taking away the tag can feel
                     like a setback, although it’s probably a deserved one.
                     However, even terrible characters can earn Karma points
                      by doing good things, so characters without the Heroic tag
                      aren’t entirely shut out. They just have to work harder at
                       earning Karma.
                           Characters can earn the Heroic tag back with a concerted
                       effort. A good first step is to make amends for their crimes
                        and to vow not to make the same mistakes. If they can
                        then prove their sincerity through their efforts, the tag
                         can be reinstated. But if they renege on their promises,
                         the tag should be removed again.
                          Changing Occupations
                          It’s okay to change traits too, especially if the character
                          decides to change occupations. Maybe they got fired
                           from their job. Or they graduated from school. Or they
                           were offered a new position.
                                When a character changes occupations, they should
                            lose the traits that came with the old occupation and
                             pick up the traits and tags of the new one. However,
                             they can hang on to the tags from their old occupation
                             if they seem to make sense. Just because they’re
                              starting a new part of their life doesn’t mean that
                              they lose all the benefits of what they did before.
                                   For instance, when Peter Parker fi rst became
                               Spider-Man, he was a high-school student. Aer he
                               graduated, he attended college for a while, continuing
                                his occupation as a student. Eventually, though, he
                                dropped out of college and began working full-time
                                as a photojournalist.
                                     As a student, Parker had the tags Mentor
                                 (Professor Curt Connors, better known as the
                                 Lizard) and Obligation: School, and the trait
                                  Quick Learner. When he finally moves on to full-
                                  time journalism, he picks up the traits Audience,
                                  Connections: Sources and Pundit. However, he
                                   loses the tag Obligation: School and the trait Quick
                                   Learner. He still maintains his friendship with
                                    Professor Connors, so he can keep the Mentor tag.
                                        In some cases, a character might have more
                                      than one occupation at a time, but they need
                                         to have a decent rationale for it. Holding
                                         on to that many occupations and having
                                       adventures at the same time is more than
                                       most people can manage.
Michael Syrett (Order #53194700)
      Changing Traits
      Even if the character doesn’t change occupations, it’s okay
      if they need to change traits from time to time, especially if
      things are changing in their life. Even so, they shouldn’t wind
      up being able to use more chosen traits than their rank allows.
      Changing the Rank Cap
      If it turns out that the players change their mind and want
      to take on bigger and more powerful challenges, go ahead
      and li the rank cap. You can just bump it up a rank or so if
      you like or remove it altogether.
           Similarly, if the players decide that they’d rather go
      back to their old kinds of adventures, you can lower the
      rank cap back to where it was—or to whatever rank best
      suits the situation.
           You can even do this with established Marvel characters
      if you like. The universe that you’re playing in is your own
      section of the Marvel Multiverse. If the characters there want
      to evolve differently than they have in the comics, go right
      ahead and let them.
      Remaking Characters
      While it’s unusual, it’s okay to let a player rebuild a character’s
      powers from scratch. This happens in the comics from time to
      time, although the character usually winds up with powers
      that are at least in the same power set as the ones that they
      started with.
          This should be a rare thing, and the player should help you
      come up with some sort of in-game reason for the remaking
      to happen. Maybe the character realized that everything they
      thought they knew about their origin story was wrong. Or
      maybe they encountered a new alien civilization or pantheon
      of gods that altered them down to their core. There are all sorts
      of possibilities, and they can lead to countless new adventures.
          Before a player remakes a character, though, they should
      consider if they really just want to come up with an entirely
      new one instead. If they’re attached to the character’s
      backstory and the history that they’ve developed in the
      game, it probably makes sense to hold on to them, but if the
      player is simply looking to try out a new set of powers or a
      new kind of character, there’s no reason they can’t make up
      a brand-new hero.
          That doesn’t mean they have to abandon their old character.
      That hero doesn’t have to die or retire or anything else. They
      can just be busy with other adventures or responsibilities
      that draw them away from the group’s endeavors, and the
      new character can step in to fill that gap.
      ENDING HEROES
      In the course of play, it’s entirely possible that the heroes are
      going to lose a fight—and one or more of them might pay
      the ultimate price. In Marvel comics, characters die all the
      time. For some, this is only a temporary setback, and that
      can be true in your game as well.
                                                                            /10/ NARRATOR
      Immortal Characters
      For some characters, death has few serious consequences.
      Gamma mutates who have access to the Green Door tag can
      come back aer a short tour through the aerlife. Mutants (or
      others) can be resurrected entirely through the Resurrection
      Protocols in use on Krakoa.

===PDFPAGE 293===
                             /10/ NARRATOR
                                In such cases, death can be traumatic, but it’s only a
                             temporary setback at best. The character dies and then
                             comes back a short while later, sometimes in a different place.
                                As a Narrator, you don’t have to worry about putting
                             such characters in mortal danger. For them, it comes with
                             the territory.
                             Killing Characters
                             With most characters, though, dying is a huge deal, and
                             you should treat it as such. Don’t have the villains in the
                             game kill a player’s character if you can help it. Leave them
                             unconscious and bleeding, near to death, but stop just shy
                             of ending them.
                                 That way the character can come back to fight another day.
                             Killing them off puts an end to that possibility—at least in
                             the short term. In a single-issue game—or even toward the
                             end of a graphic-novel adventure—that may be fine. It can
                             even make the session more memorable than ever.
                                 In an ongoing series, however, this can be a big problem.
                             The player is going to want to come back to play in the next
                             session, and the death of their character puts a large crimp
                             in those plans.
                                 That said, if the player is up for their character dying,
                             don’t hesitate to go along with it. Give the character their
                             moment in the spotlight for their big exit. Allow them to
                             inspire the remaining characters to soldier on without them.
                             Let them give the character’s death meaning.
                                 Then—when you have the time—pull the player aside
                             and begin plotting for what’s going to happen for them next.

Michael Syrett (Order #53194700)
      Shattering Characters
      The same guidelines apply for shattering characters,
      although this is a bit easier to come back from, and the
      player can keep control of the character throughout the
      experience if they like. However, not every player is
      interested in role-playing a character whose psyche has
      been shattered. In that case, just let the mental health
      professionals cart the character away with the promise
      that they might return at some future date.
          If the player decides to stick with the character, let them
      do so for as long as they like. If they get tired of showing how
      broken their character has become, they can let them go for
      a bit, just as if the character has been killed.
      The Wipeout
      It’s not common, but it’s entirely possible to kill off every
      member of a team all at once. If you’re being careful with
      the characters, this is unlikely, but if it happens, you have
      some big decisions to make.
           The first thing to do is ask your players how they feel
      about it. Do they want those characters back, or would they
      rather start over? Either way is okay.
           If the players see this as an opportunity to make a change,
      roll with it. Have them make up or pick new characters, and
      then bring them right back into the adventure. Just because
      one team of heroes failed doesn’t mean that the villains
      win. It means that someone else has to step up to stop the
      villains instead.
           If the players would like to keep playing their current
      characters, see later in this section for guidelines on
      how to bring them back from the dead. There’s one other
      option when an entire team is wiped out though: The
      villains save them.
           Most times, if a single character is killed, the other heroes
      drive off the villain and try to recover their teammate’s
      remains. If all the characters are downed, though, the
      villain might see this as an opportunity to capture them
      all instead. Rather than dying, they can all wake up in
      captivity, their wounds bound and cared for by the people
      they were fighting against.
           If the entire team is shattered instead—or some
      combination of such terrible fates—the heroes could wake
      up to find themselves in a treatment facility for the mentally
      ill. Managing to recover and then escape could be the basis
      of an unforgettable adventure.
      Meanwhile
      While a character is killed or shattered, there’s the matter of
      what their player should do until the character is ready to
      return. The first thing to do is discuss with the player how
      long the character should be absent. If they have some way
      to come back right away, then go ahead and work your way
      through that process.
          If the character doesn’t have an instant way to come
      back, then bringing them back can become the focus of the
      game from that point on. The heroes can work together to
      figure out what really happened to the character and what
      it might take to get them to return.

                             otherwise occupied somewhere else.
                       ▶ The character became unmoored in time

                       ▶ The character’s mind was absorbed by

                             needs to be restored to an appropriate body.
                        Once you figure that out, you can work out how the
                    character might return to the game—and what the
                    player might do in the meantime. If the player won’t
                    be without their character for long, they could just be
                    patient and hold on for a bit, perhaps helping you out by
                    playing a character the Narrator is normally in charge of.

                    disappear for longer, then the player should join the
                    game with a new character. That can be one of their own
                    design or an established Marvel character, as they prefer.
                        However, be sure that you discuss with the player what
                    should happen with this second character if and when the
                    first one comes back. Will the player keep playing the new
                    character, or will they go back to the old one? Will the one
                    they don’t choose to play die? Or become a character that
                    you control as the Narrator? Or will they simply leave now
                    that their purpose is complete?

                    and memorable, you should do the same for their return.
                    This should be a momentous experience for the entire team.
                        If a supposedly dead character just shows back up on the
                    doorstep of the heroes’ headquarters, do they know what
                    happened to them while they were gone, or does their return
                    present a mystery yet to be solved? Or did the rest of the
                    team have to go on an epic adventure to discover what really

                    and revives in the place where they died, usually taking on
                    some kind of twisted and grotesque form in the course of

                 PLAYING IN THE MULTIVERSE
                 When you play this game, remember that you don’t need to
                 follow any particular bit of continuity from Marvel comics
                 or any other source. The universe that the characters are
                 playing in is unique to them, and you don’t need to feel
                 beholden to anything else.
                     That can be both freeing and terrifying, but don’t fret.
                 One of the wonderful things about playing a game based on
                 Marvel comics is that you don’t have to do all that work on
                 your own. You have more than 80 years of published stories
                 that you can draw upon as much as you like.
                     Because of that, you don’t have to build out the world
                 at all. You can add on to it, but the assumed default for
                 everything in your game is that it matches everything in
                 the comics. You have only to concern yourself with where
                 things differ in your game.
                 Making Your Universe Your Own
                 Once you start making your mark on the Marvel Multiverse,
                 it’s hard to stop. Everything that you and your players do in
                 the game makes your version of it that much more real for
                 you and for them. The further you go along that path, the
                 more your version feels like your own.
                      As you go, take some time to keep track of the things
                 that have happened and the decisions you’ve made that
                 are different from the Earth-616 continuity. In this way, you
                 and your players form the continuity of your own universe.
                      If one of the other players seems up for it, you can assign
                 the duty of keeping track of things to them. If you spot one
                 of the players taking notes about everything as you narrate
Michael Syrett (Order #53194700)
      the game, they are the perfect person for that gig. They’re
      already keeping track of things for themselves, so you might
      as well make it official.
          Having a good set of notes can help a lot when you’re
      planning out your adventures and how you think the
      characters’ story might go. It keeps you from having to
      recreate things you might have already created on the fly, and
      it gives your slice of the Marvel Multiverse a sense of realism.
          As you play the game—especially if you move into
      ongoing-series mode—the little decisions you make early
      on can start to add up. The places you design, the names you
      give the characters, the relationships between them—all
      that can be a lot to keep track of, but that’s also what helps
      make your game sessions uniquely yours.
      Continuity
      It also means that you’re not wrong when you say that
      something in your game’s universe differs from the way it
      is for Earth-616. Those little details start to add up to form
      the history—the continuity—of your game’s universe. You
      just have to keep track of them.
          If that sounds like a hassle, it’s really only as important as
      you make it. If you contradict yourself at one point or another,
      you have a couple of options. You can confess to the mistake.
      Or you can explain how you weren’t actually wrong at all.
          Comic-book writers have a long tradition of retroactively
      repairing continuity errors, called retconning. You should
      feel free to do the same.
          In fact, Stan Lee had a tradition of giving out a No-Prize
      to readers of Marvel comics who pointed out a problem in
      the stories’ continuity and then came up with a plausible
      explanation for it. You can do the same, enlisting your
      players’ help.
          Instead of awarding a No-Prize, though—which was
      literally nothing—you can give them a point of Karma for
      their efforts and for helping keep everything on track.
      Point of Divergence
      The moment you start a game session, you will diverge from
      the standard Marvel comics continuity. The fact that your
      players are doing something new in the setting and have
      characters making their own choices and having an impact
      is bound to do that.
          The question then becomes at what point do things begin
      to differ? And that’s really up to you.
          You don’t have to be a Marvel comics historian to run
      the game. Few people have read all of the Marvel stories
      ever published, much less have committed them to memory.
      Your world can just be your impression of the Marvel Comics
      setting, as detailed or as fuzzy as you want it to be.
          If you’re a stickler for details, you can set a moment in
      time and say that everything until then is the same in your
      game as it was in the comics. Like right aer the Super-Hero
      Civil War. Or maybe aer the Secret Wars and the birth of
      the Eighth Cosmos. Or whenever you like.
      Keeping Up to Date
      If you’re a big Marvel comics fan, you might want to keep
      your world up to date with what’s happening in the comics
      in real time. This can be a bit of a challenge, especially since
294
===PDFPAGE 296===
                    you don’t know how things are going to turn out in the stories
                    until they’re complete.
                        Instead, it’s easier to simply use big Marvel crossover
                    events as milestones. Think of them as beacons that you
                    and the other players can steer by.
                        For instance, in 2022, Marvel had a big event that involved
                    most of their comics, called A.X.E.: Judgment Day. It brought the
                    Avengers, X-Men and Eternals together in a world-shaking
                    disaster in which a Celestial known as the Progenitor decided
                    to judge every person on the planet to see if the Earth was
                    worth saving or needed to be destroyed.
                        Even if your players have read the comics and know how
                    the overall event comes out, this sort of event offers a chance
                    to have your game cross over with the comics too. You can
                    play out an adventure in which the characters have to deal
                    with the trials that the Progenitor places before them. This
                    is a great way to both explore the nature of those characters
                    and to feel connected to the wider Marvel Multiverse.
                        Or you can ignore all that. You can say it never happened
                    in your game’s universe, or you can say it all happened
                    at some point, but the
                    characters survived it.

      GAME STYLE
      Marvel comics offers up all sorts of different types of stories,
      and you can do the same in your game. It’s worth taking a
      bit of time before you start playing—or even as the game
      progresses—to see what kinds of stories your players are
      interested in. This is called your game’s style.
      Action
      The default style for a Marvel comics story is action. These
      games are full of brawls and banter and are packed from one
      end to the other with all sorts of opportunities for thrilling
      adventure. Pick up most Marvel comics, and you can find
      yourself deep inside an action story in no time at all.
          Action stories tend to concentrate on the plot and the life-
      threatening stakes that go alongside it rather than exploring
      the inner lives and motivations of the characters. There’s
      nothing saying that you can’t do both, of course, but when a
      herald of Galactus arrives in New York City and announces
      that their boss is on his way to feast on the planet’s energy,
      most other concerns get put aside.
          To make an action story more than a set of plot points
      that the heroes race through from one to the next, though,
      you need to give the heroes some downtime in between to
      let them breathe. To have those human moments that make
      the stakes that they’re fighting for feel more meaningful.

                                          Otherwise, the players may start to think the characters’
                                          only worth comes from how well they make their dice rolls.
                                             It’s also important to allow the characters to fail. When it
                                          seems like everything is on the line, letting the characters
                                          blow it might seem like the worst of all possible outcomes, but
                                          that’s okay. Some of the most memorable stories in Marvel
                                          comics happen aer the heroes failed.
                                          Examples: Look to many of the Avengers titles for stories
                                          like these. Epic adventures that ride along the razor’s
                                          edge of action.
                                          Comedy
                                          One of the greatest strengths of Marvel comics is their humor.
                                          Many of their stories do a fantastic job of leavening the most
                                          serious and dangerous of moments with a sense of levity and
                                          fun. If you like, you can lean way into that, highlighting the
                                          funnier parts of the stories—putting the comic in comic books.
                                              This works well if you and your players already enjoy
                                          each other’s senses of humor. If you’re all on the same
                                          wavelength most of the time, it’s easy to get your friends
                                          to laugh. If you have to force it, though, it can fall flat, so be
                                          careful how far you push it.
                                              Even if you and the players are all rolling around on the
                                          floor and clutching your sides, there should still be a plot for
                                             them to sink their teeth into. Something that motivates
                                               them to move along and gives them something new
                                                to joke about every so oen. Otherwise, the game can
                                                 quickly devolve into nothing but zingers, and eventu-
                                                 ally, that gets dull.
                                                      Keep the players moving while they’re laughing,
                                                    though, and you can entertain each other for years.
                                                    Examples: Spider-Man (Peter Parker) has a
                                                     notorious sense of humor that plays out in most
                                                      of his tales, oen to the great irritation of his foes.
                                                       Deadpool, She-Hulk and Gwenpool lean hard
                                                       on the humor as well, even including breaking
                                                       the fourth wall to speak directly to the reader.
                                                            Mystery
                                                              Another common genre in Marvel comics is
                                                              mystery. Most of the stories aren’t labeled
                                                             as such, but if you find yourself wondering
                                                         who committed a crime and how and why
                                                      they did it, you just found yourself in the middle
                                                       of a mystery.
                                                              Characters oen find themselves in such
                                                            situations by accident. Someone attacks them,
                                                             and they don’t know why. They hear screams
                                                            and rush to help those in need, but there’s
                                                          something deeper going on.
                                                               The presence of super-powers and the
                                                           supernatural can make many such mysteries
                                                           difficult to solve. Locked-door mysteries get
                                                             a little wilder if you consider that someone
                                                             could have phased through the walls or
                                                              teleported in from the next block over.
                                                                   Even so, a bit of mystery can serve as a
                                                                good way to slow down the action for a bit
                                                                and ask the characters to work with their
                                                                 minds rather than their fists. This can

===PDFPAGE 298===
                    actually be more engaging for the players, as they usually
                    wind up doing a lot of the figuring on their own rather than
                    relying on their characters’ skills in combat.
                    Examples: Jessica Jones’ work as a private investigator puts
                    her in the heart of mysteries all the time, but you can also
                    look to the mental gymnastics characters like Mister Fantastic
                    use to figure out what’s going on behind the action in their
                    fantastic adventures.
                    Romance
                    Marvel used to publish romance comic books many decades
                    ago, but those sorts of stories—along with Westerns and
                    war stories—fell out of popularity a long time ago. You can
                    include elements of those in your adventures, of course, but
                    of those choices, what adds a bit of flavor to many super-hero
                    stories is a bit of interpersonal romance.
                        When you have lots of attractive characters running
                    around with other attractive characters, some feelings for
                    each other are bound to crop up from time to time. They
                    might even arise for characters on the other side of the law,
                    just to complicate things even more.
                        If you’re going to incorporate romantic elements in your
                    game beyond casual flirting, be sure to take the temperature
                    of the other players. Not everyone is comfortable with such
                    things and might consider them distractions from the more
                    important elements of the game. Others, however, might
                    love playing around with romance like that and feel that
                    these bits actually are the most important parts of the game.
                    Examples: Many stories of the X-Men involve not just
                    action-packed, high-stakes plots but also a great read of
                    interpersonal romance. This does a great job of breaking up
                    the perilous moments and also of reminding the characters
                    who and what it is they’re actually fighting for.
                    Gritty
                    Many stories become more serious, grim and gritty. They
                    involve ill-fated heroes being reluctantly dragged into saving
                    people who are even more doomed. These stories tend to
                    involve smaller teams or even single heroes who have a lot
                    of dead-serious internal dialogue.
                        In these stories, the heroes oen aren’t trying to save the
                    world. Most of the time, they’re lucky if they can manage to
                    save themselves and maybe have a sliver of hope of doing a
                    lick of good in the world for the people they care about most.
                        These stories oen make for engrossing ways to explore
                    the deepest parts of a character’s motivations and see what
                    really makes them tick. They can sometimes be a little too
                    intense for players who are more interested in nonstop action
                    rather than high drama.
                    Examples: Wolverine (Logan) is the classic gritty character.
                    Many Daredevil stories run along these noirish lines as
                    well. In the end, stories that don’t turn out well for anyone
                    involved fit right in here.
                    Horror
                    If the gritty tales aren’t dark enough for your tastes, you
                    can make your way into full-blown horror instead. In these
                    stories, the heroes aren’t concerned with saving the world
                    as much as they are with getting out alive. With their own
                                                                                      2
Michael Syrett (Order #53194700)
     lives starkly on the line, you can see what’s really the most
     important to them, as well as how they feel about what
     they’ve done with their lives.
     Examples: Some characters are built for horror from the
     start, like the Man-Thing or Werewolf by Night. Others—like
     Blade—find fighting against the horrors in the world to be
     a core part of their purpose.
     Mix It Up
     There’s nothing that says you can’t mix and match among the
     genres as much as you like in your game. The classic Marvel
     comics way is to lean into the action and spice it up with hints
     of all of the other types of stories from time to time. That keeps
     the challenges fresh and keeps the characters from falling into
     a rut in which they can start to predict what happens next.
         A good Narrator tries to always keep the players guessing
     about what’s around the corner, and by coming up with your
     own blend of styles and varying it up from time to time, you
     can deliver that to them.
     DESIGNING ADVENTURES
     While there will be official published adventures out there
     for you to run for your players, many Narrators eventually
     decide to try their hand at designing adventures. This is a
     fantastic idea and can be amazing fun. You are likely to do
     a wonderful job of it. Aer all, no one knows your players
     and their characters as well as you do.
         You probably have all sorts of ideas for how you want
     your games to go, and you should run with those and have
     fun with them. As you go, though, here’s some hopefully
     helpful advice.
     No Plan Survives
     As the old saying goes, no plan survives contact with the
     enemy. The other players in your game are not your enemies,
     of course, but they are certain to lay waste to the plans you
     have for your game with regularity and abandon.
         That, of course, is the point. That’s the thing that
     separates tabletop role-playing games from other forms of
     entertainment: the way the players react to and riff off the
     Narrator’s plans.
         If you want to just tell the other players a story, you can
     write it down and read it to them. They don’t have to be
     any more involved than a live audience for your tale. They
     might even love that.
         But a game like this is not about telling a story to your
     friends. It’s about concocting one with them.
         It’s not your job to put the plot on rails and run the
     characters through it. That sort of thinking tells the players
     that they’re just acting out predestined parts in a story that
     was always fated to go one way, no matter what they hoped
     to contribute.
         A better way to look at your responsibilities as the
     Narrator is to present your fellow players with a challenge
                                                                          /10/ NARRATOR
     and see what they do to solve it. You don’t have to know how
     they’re going to rise to that challenge. You might have some
     good guesses, and you should prepare for each one of those,
     but don’t work at it too hard.
         Let your players surprise you. The stories you’re creating
     together aren’t just for them. They’re for you too.
97
===PDFPAGE 299===
                  /10/ NARRATOR
                 Prepare, but Not Too Much
                 Since it’s hard to create a coherent narrative in your
                 adventures without your players’ help, the best thing you
                 can do is enlist them to help you with the job. The simplest
                 way to do this is to prepare the adventure before you start.
                     In most cases, you shouldn’t plan the adventure down
                 to the last detail, though. If you put hours’, days’ or even
                 weeks’ worth of work into an adventure, when the players
                 do something you didn’t anticipate, you may be tempted to
                 force them down the path you’d planned out rather than let
                 them have as much influence as they should.
                     It’s best to have a solid framework in mind and to
                 understand not just what the characters you control are
                 doing but why. That way when the adventure goes in a
                 different direction, you should have a good idea about how
                 to make it all pivot.
                     Done well, the players might never even notice. They
                 oen think that you’ve planned it that way all along!
                Time to Plot
                 To start out, you should pick a villain (or villains)—which
                 we’ll get to in a bit—and come up with a plot for them. You
                 can do this in either order. Some Narrators like to match the
                 heroes up against villains first, while others like to come up
                 with the plot first.
                    When mulling over your plot, ask yourself a number of
                 questions. Designing a crime is kind of like solving a mystery
                 but in reverse, because you get to come up with the answers
                 you like best.
                     In a traditional investigation of a crime, the classic three
                 questions that detectives ask are about whether or not the
                 suspect had the motive, the means and the opportunity to
                 commit the crime. You need to supply all three of those to
                 your villain.
                     ▶ What is the villain aer? Money, power, love? It
                          should be something they can’t get through ethical
                          means. That’s what makes them a villain, aer all,
                          rather than someone who does an honest day’s work
                          to get what they want.
                     ▶ What are they willing to do to get it? The easy
                          answer is “anything,” but think about the
                          particulars in this case. Are they ready to infect
                          a city with an illness? Rob elderly folks? Harm
                          children? Kill innocents? Punch a hole into
                          another universe?
                     ▶ Who is in their way? Is it the law? Their rivals? The
                          heroes? Reality itself?
                     ▶ Why now? What happened that made the villain
                          need to do this now? If they weren’t committing
                          these crimes last week, what changed? Is this a
                          new opportunity that presented itself—perhaps an
                          unforeseen result of the heroes’ previous actions?
                          Or was the villain planning this for a long time, and
                          now they’re finally ready?
                     Playing around with these questions, you might come
                 up with all sorts of potential plots. That’s great. Just take
                 some notes on them and figure out which one appeals
                 to you most.
Michael Syrett (Order #53194700)
      Make It Personal
      The best adventures are ones in which the stakes are so high
      that the heroes are instantly motivated to help. Sure, they
      want to stop the bank robbery because someone might get
      hurt, but if they know the people who work in the bank, their
      fears for them become much more concrete.
         Even the most altruistic heroes feel the tension rise when
      the fate of people they know and care about is on the line.
      Then it’s not whether someone gets hurt but whether someone
      important to them gets hurt.
         If the villain is someone the hero has a history with, that
      can make it more personal too. When Spider-Man (Peter
      Parker) fights the Green Goblin (Norman Osborn), Spider-
      Man remembers all the horrible things the Green Goblin has
      done to him and his friends in the past. That spurs him on
      even harder to put a stop to the Goblin’s plans.
      The Hook
      Once you have the plot worked out—or at least a framework
      for it—and how to make the stakes personal for the heroes,
      you need to figure out how the heroes get involved in
      the adventure.
          In many cases, the villain doesn’t want to draw the heroes’
      attention, as they would rather commit their crimes in secret
      instead. But they can’t control every circumstance. Mistakes
      get made, and evidence of their activities gets out.
          Maybe someone they captured gets away. Or someone they
      thought they killed recovers. Or one of their underlings sees
      how horrible they are and has a change of heart.
          That’s where the heroes come in. They can follow these
      clues back to the villain and confront them—hopefully
      before it’s already too late.
          You don’t have to work too hard at this if you don’t want
      to. Sometimes, the heroes get wind of the villain’s plans from
      the police. Or they see it on the news.
          If you want to be even more straightforward about it, the
      villain can attack the heroes directly. If the villain sees the
      heroes as the biggest obstacle to their plans, they might want
      to cross defeating them off their list straightaway. They can
      ambush the heroes themselves. Or they can hire someone
      else to do it. Or they can stand in front of the heroes and
      challenge them to a fight. It’s up to them—and you!
      Plot Points
      Now you know what the villain is up to, who’s at risk and
      how the heroes get involved. Aer that, it’s a matter of trying
      to guess how the heroes will respond.
          While you can’t know exactly what the heroes will do, you
      can make some decent guesses, and you can help that out
      by pointing them in the right direction. First, though, you
      need to know what the right direction is.
          By now, you probably have a starting point and an ending
      point. The trick is to figure out what happens in between.
          If you’re creating a single issue, you don’t need too many
      twists and turns between the beginning and the end. You
      want to create a self-contained story in a single session, so
      you need to think in terms of what you can fit into the time
      you have. As a rule of thumb, you probably have time for one
      major encounter every hour or two of play. That means in a
      four-hour session, you might have two or three encounters.
298
===PDFPAGE 300===
                        These encounters form plot points that you can either list
                    out in a row or even diagram out with a flowchart. Aer each
                    encounter, you should have clues that lead the characters
                    to the next plot point or—better yet—give them a choice
                    of two or three different plot points they can head toward.
                        You should mark the plot points that cannot be skipped
                    as essential. These are things that the heroes must manage
                    to do in order to proceed through the plot. Sometimes they
                    can do one of a few different things to advance, but you
                    should make sure you know which plot points they involve.
                        Other plot points can be optional. The heroes can get
                    to them if they have the time and inclination. They can
                    illuminate the story and give it and the characters involved
                    more depth. But they can be skipped over if the players would
                    like to do something else—or if you’re running short on time.
                        You can add in optional plot points on the fly. If the players
                    decide they want to do something you hadn’t planned for,
                    go ahead and let them. Eventually, you can hope to get them
                    back to one of the essential plot points they need to hit, but
                    there’s no need to force them straight there.
                        In fact, if you can manage it, you can even substitute in
                    some of those new plot points for some of the essential ones.
                    The simplest way to do that is to steal some of the important
                    bits from an essential plot point and blend them in with the
                    new one the players led you to.
                    Bigger Plots
                    If you’re creating a graphic novel, you have a lot more room
                    to work with. You can play out the story over several sessions
                    and lead up to a bigger ending.
                        Ideally, each play session forms a single issue of its own
                    with a complete story, and all together, the series of them
                    build up to that graphic novel. That way, the players get the
                    sense of accomplishment of completing that single story on
                    their way toward reaching the end of the larger plot.
Michael Syrett (Order #53194700)
                                                                                         Ponsor
                                                                tano Carlucci & Justin
                                    Art by Sara Pichelli, Gae
           You don’t even have to tell the players that you’re working
       toward a graphic-novel plot. You can just present a series of
       single issues to them and watch them as they start to figure
       out the overarching plot linking those individual stories
       into a greater tale.
           You can handle an ongoing series in much the same way.
       Present the players with groups of single issues that every
       so oen collectively form a graphic novel. When they finish
       one, you can move on to another, building on the stories
       that you’ve played through before, just like you’re creating
       sequel aer sequel.
           If you like, you can break up an ongoing series with actual
       standalone single issues too. This gives you a chance to try
       out new ideas and to take a break from the ongoing story
       without leaving it behind.
       Setups and Payoffs
        An important thing to consider when playing through
        adventures with your players is that people expect their
        stories to have setups and payoffs, even when they’re playing
        a game like this.
            A setup is the foreshadowing you do in a story. The bread
        crumbs you leave for the players to follow through the tale.
        The clues you leave to what’s actually going on that you
        then let the players figure out. When they do put everything
        together and realize what’s happening—when they get to
        the big reveal—that’s the payoff.
            A payoff without a setup feels hollow. Instead of saying,
       “Wow! Now it all makes sense!” the players say, “What? Where
                                                                                         /10/ NARRATOR
        did that come from?” They need to be able to look back at
        what’s come before and see how it all led to this point, even
        if they didn’t know it at the time.
            Similarly, setups without payoffs can lead to frustration.
        If you just scatter clues all over the place—things that leave
        questions in the players’ minds—and they never learn what
        those clues mean, that irritates them. They oen ask what
 299
===PDFPAGE 301===
                  /10/ NARRATOR
                 was going on and why you bothered to drop those hints for
                 them if they didn’t mean anything, because they feel misled.
                     Players oen take everything the Narrator says as a setup.
                 They’re trained to look for hints like these, and sometimes
                 they can seem to concoct them out of nothing. An offhand
                 remark you make about something innocuous can point
                 them in a whole different direction than what you intended.
                     Because of this, you should be careful with how you
                 reveal clues and answer questions. It’s perfectly fine to leave
                 red herrings—false clues—around for the heroes to find if
                 they’re intended to confuse them and keep them guessing
                 about what’s really happening. Just be judicious with them.
                 A little goes a long way.
                 Course Correction
                 If the players somehow latch on to something that has
                 nothing to do with the plot, you have two choices.
                     First, you can be blunt with the players and tell them
                 that they’re making a mistake. The “clue” they spotted isn’t
                 a clue and has nothing to do with the plot. This may not be
                 the most artful way to handle it, but it can prevent people
                 from wasting time on something that you know isn’t going
                 to lead anywhere.
                     Second—and far more challenging and interesting—you
                 can incorporate the error into the plot. That little detail the
                 players sunk their teeth into might have meant nothing
                 at the time, but they don’t know that. If you can work that
                 into your plot—or even come up with a whole new plot to fit
                 it—it can lead you to all sorts of new and unexpected places.
                     Think of such things as inspiration for the adventures.
                 One of the best things that separates role-playing games from
                 other sorts of entertainment is that you can do things like
                 this. You can roll off in different directions on the slightest
                 of inspiration and see where you wind up. Few other things
                 can replicate that.
                 Playing with Expectations
                 If your players are good about spotting setups and looking
                 for payoffs, you can play with their expectations—and you
                 should. If players get exactly what they’re expecting to
                 happen every time, they can become bored with the story, as it
                 then feels like the whole thing’s rolling toward an inevitable
                 finish that everyone can see coming from miles away.
                     When possible, give the players setups that are ambiguous.
                 If they can lead to more than one conclusion, that’s not a
                 mystery solved but a mystery presented. You should, of
                 course, know what the correct conclusion is, but leaving the
                 players uncertain keeps their interest.
                     As the players discuss the setup, listen to what they
                 have to say. They might come to the correct conclusion
                 straightaway, but you don’t have to let them know that. Hold
                 on to the secret for at least a little bit longer.
                     If the players are constantly figuring out what’s happening
                 ahead of time, you can change things on the fly. If they strike
                 upon the right solution but you have other viable options,
                 you can switch over to one of those other options without
                 telling them.
                     Be careful not to abuse this ability. If the players are sharp
                 and pick up on clues fast, let them revel in their success. But
                 every now and then, you should throw them a twist to help
                 keep them on their toes.
Michael Syrett (Order #53194700)
         You can even purposefully mislead the characters. The
      villain can plant evidence that implicates someone else.
      Witnesses can lie about what they’ve seen, either out of
      fear of the villain or for reasons of their own. Part of the
      adventure then becomes having the heroes sort through
      that misinformation to find the truth.
      BALANCING COMBATS
      In their adventures, characters are likely to wind up in a
      fight. As a Narrator, it can be tricky to balance such combats
      so that they are a challenge to the characters without being
      overwhelming. There are all sorts of different contexts that
      can affect a fight, and it’s difficult to account for them.
          However, here are some guidelines to use as a basis.
      Matching Ranks
      The simplest way to balance a combat is to match every
      character on the players’ side with a foe of equal rank on the
      other side. Some powers are going to be more applicable than
      others in any given situation, so this isn’t a perfect solution,
      but it works most of the time.
          The trick with that, of course, is that such fights are so
      evenly matched that the heroes are just as likely to lose as
      win. That’s the sort of battle you should probably save for
      the end of an adventure.
          Rather than matching heroes up with villains of the
      same rank, you can mix things up a bit. As a rule of thumb,
      you can match a character of any rank against two foes
      of the next lower rank or four foes of a rank two less than
      theirs and so on.
      Example: Black Panther (T’Challa) is evenly matched against
      Killmonger, as they are both Rank 4. He would also be evenly
      matched against the Red Skull and Crossbones, as the two
      villains are Rank 3.
      Initial Fights
      Not every fight should be evenly matched. Sometimes—
      especially early in an adventure—the heroes take on foes
      they should be able to easily defeat. In such cases, it’s fine to
      pit the characters against foes of much lower rank.
          To keep things interesting, you should vary the situations
      in which the fights happen. Few battles should be as simple
      as having the heroes stand toe-to-toe with their opponents.
      Battling through a crowded city street, a busy office building
      or even a skyscraper construction site can offer all sorts of
      new opportunities to flex powers and try out new tactics,
      both for the Narrator and the heroes.
          Additionally, you can try throwing waves of weaker
      opponents at the heroes and seeing how they handle them.
      As you test out the team, you should get a better idea of their
      capabilities and what you can throw at them in the future.
      Doomed to Lose
      It’s okay to set up battles that the heroes are doomed to lose.
      Sometimes the greatest moments that heroes have are aer
      they get pounded into the dirt by a superior force. This
      encourages them to seek out other solutions or maybe even
      to call in other heroes to help.
           If you’re going to smack the heroes around like this,
      though, you need to give them a means of escape. It’s not
300
===PDFPAGE 302===
                    fair to toss them into a death trap with no way to avoid
                    their ultimate fate—unless, of course, death isn’t terribly
                    permanent for them. Most of the time, though, they should
                    have a way to practice discretion and get out while the
                    getting is good.
                        However, you should set up battles like this rarely.
                    While they can be a great way to demonstrate a foe’s power
                    and superiority to set the stage for later in the adventure,
                    few players enjoy watching their characters get beaten
                    down regularly.
                    Climactic Battles
                    Climactic battles—the ones that come at the end of a story,
                    whether it’s a single issue or a graphic novel—require
                    planning. Try to think about the situation from the
                    perspective of the villain. They’re not showing up at the
                    appointed time just to give the heroes a punching bag. Most
                    of the time, they’re going to attempt to tilt the circumstances
                    around the battle in their favor.
                        Consider not only where the battle should take place but
                    what kinds of help the villain should arrange for themselves.
                    Many villains—like Kingpin or the Red Skull—surround
                    themselves with soldiers or underlings to handle their
                    security and take care of pesky things like heroes for them.
                    They step into a fight only when forced to do it. Others—like
                    Kraven the Hunter or Carnage—enjoy the thrill of battle and
                    seek it out at every opportunity.
                        For a venue, think big. Give the heroes and the villains
                    a chance to stretch their abilities and let loose. It could be
                    atop a Helicarrier, atop Avengers Mountain or deep in the
                    Negative Zone. Or pick a spectacular and important real-
                    world location, like the Statue of Liberty, Times Square or
                    the White House.
Michael Syrett (Order #53194700)
      When the Battle Ends
      When setting up a battle, you should think about what
      happens aerward. Where might the heroes go next, and
      what will lead them there to do that? If possible, give them
      a few choices so they feel like they have some agency over
      what happens.
          Many Narrators plan for what happens if the characters
      do what they expect—which is usually to win. But you should
      also have a backup plan for what happens if things resolve
      differently. What if the heroes lose? Or run away? Or avoid
      the conflict entirely?
                                                              Art by Paul Renaud
          The plans don’t necessarily have to diverge much. Win
      or lose, many of the same things can happen. If the heroes
      are le scattered and unconscious, they might recover to
      discover many of the same things they would have if they
      had triumphed. But you should think about how that might
      happen so you’re prepared for any outcome.
      TIMES AND PLACES
      As the Narrator, it’s up to you to set up the adventures for the
      other players. The default setting is now, oen in Manhattan,
      but you can change that around as you like.
          Higher-rank characters tend to travel more, as they can
      confront troubles that threaten many more people. Many
                                                                          /10/ NARRATOR
      such adventures take the heroes all around the world or
      even to distant galaxies or other dimensions or universes.
          For original characters, however, it can be fun to set the
      adventures in your actual hometown. You likely know the
      place better than any other part of the world, so instead of
      having to learn about Manhattan or Wakanda, you can rely
      on the knowledge that’s already in your head.
