                 Origin Stories
                 If you’re starting out with original heroes
                 at Rank 1, you can start the adventure with the
                 characters’ origins. You might even begin with
                 them before they get their powers.
                     The main question in such stories is: How did
                 the characters get their powers? Are they all from
                 the same source, which would link the characters
                 together naturally because of that? If their origins
                 all spring from different things, what brings them
                 together here and now? What common threat do they face
                 that unites them?
                     Ideally, this is not just a single event but an ongoing
                 problem. This gives the heroes a good reason to work with
                 each other on a regular basis rather than going their separate
                 ways at the adventure’s end.
                 Flashbacks
                 Even if you’re working with established Marvel characters,
                 you don’t have to remain in the present day. Your game’s
                 continuity is your own. If you want to play with the original
                 X-Men as teenagers under Professor X’s tutelage at Xavier’s
                 School for Gied Youngsters, go right ahead. If the players
                 want to adventure as the Invaders during World War II, that’s
                 what you should do.
                    You don’t have to make your entire game about this,
                 though. You can, instead, flash back to those days for a single
                 issue or a graphic novel or however long you like. This can
                 be a great chance to explore a secret origin, perhaps tying
                 an original character’s roots to established Marvel history.
                    For an example in Marvel comics, look to Silk, a character
                 who was introduced more than 40 years aer Peter Parker
                 became Spider-Man. Despite that, she was there the day
                 Parker was bitten by a radioactive spider, and her powers
                 are tied to his because of that.
                 Days of Future Past
                 Of course, the past and the present aren’t your only options.
                 You can adventure in one of Marvel’s potential futures or
                 alternate histories as well.
                     If you decide to do this, you should think about whether
                 the heroes are from that alternate universe or are just
                 visiting it. In other words, do they consider that their core
                 reality or not? Is the entire series going to be set there, or
                 might the heroes hit other parts of the Multiverse?
                     Either way, since that universe is a different part of the
                 Multiverse from Earth-616, the heroes don’t have to worry
                 about accidentally changing the timeline in the main Marvel
                 Universe and winding up in another alternate universe if
                 and when they return to that.
                 Using Events
                 You should feel free to set your game in any part of Marvel’s
                 illustrious history. The most attractive eras are oen based
                 around one of the major crossover events that shook up the
                 comics. This includes things like:
                    ▶ Age of Ultron
                    ▶ Annihilation
                    ▶ Civil War
                    ▶ Civil War II
Michael Syrett (Order #53194700)
a
            ▶ Contest of Champions
            ▶ Dark Phoenix Saga
            ▶ Dark Reign
            ▶ House of M
            ▶ Infinity Gauntlet
            ▶ Judgment Day
            ▶ Kree/Skrull War
            ▶ Secret Empire
            ▶ Secret Invasion
            ▶ Secret Wars (1984)
            ▶ Secret Wars (2016)
            ▶ Spider-Island
            ▶ Spider-Verse
            ▶ War of the Realms
            ▶ World War Hulk
            ▶ X of Swords
              If you know what all those are, you deserve a No-Prize!
          If you want to read them to find out what you might have
          missed, a subscription to Marvel Unlimited is a great bargain.
              If your players don’t know what happened during the
          event you choose, you can use the plot verbatim. Just be sure
          to caution them against going back to read those events and
          spoiling things for themselves and the rest of the players.
              If the players do know the event—and even if they don’t—
          you should feel free to change things around to better fit
          their team and to play with their expectations. Just because
          it happened one way in the comics—on Earth-616—doesn’t
          mean it has to go the same in your world. Aer all, the heroes
          in your game are bound to have some sort of influence on
          the outcome.
              If you don’t want to tackle a massive event, you can
          instead concoct an adventure that is related to it but wasn’t
          featured in the comics. Think of it as an untold story that
          finally gets its day in your game.
          FILLING OUT THE CAST
          In the course of a good adventure, the heroes don’t just battle
          villains but encounter all sorts of different people. When you’re
          setting up an adventure—and particularly with an ongoing
          series—it’s worth taking some time to fill out the rest of the cast.
              You don’t have to tackle this task on your own. Enlist the
          players and ask them to tell you about the most important
          people in their characters’ lives.
    302
===PDFPAGE 304===
                    Friends and Family
                    The people who heroes interact with most are their friends
                    and family. Think about the following questions:
                        ▶ Who are the hero’s parents?
                        ▶ What do they do?
                        ▶ Does the hero have siblings? Cousins? Other
                             important relatives?
                        ▶ Who lives in the hero’s house?
                        ▶ Who does the hero hang out with when
                             given a choice?
                        ▶ Does the hero live on their own? With friends? With
                             their family? Some other situation?
                        ▶ Does the hero have children of their own?
                    Work Friends
                    Another thing to consider is what the heroes do for a living.
                    Aer friends and family, the people who many folks interact
                    with the most are those they work with.
                       Most players already put a bit of thought into this when
                    they came up with their hero’s occupation as part of creating
                    their backstory. However, it can help to delve a little bit
                    deeper into it.
                        ▶ Does the hero have to work? Does someone support
                             them? Are they independently wealthy?
                        ▶ Does the hero have a boss? Co-workers? Employees?
                             Others in a position of authority over them, like a
                             teacher or principal?
                        ▶ Who does the hero interact with as part of their
                             occupation? Customers? Clients? Teachers?
                             Fellow students?
                    Romance
                    Romantic relationships play a huge role in the lives of many
                    teenagers and adults. The characters in your game are likely
                    no exception.
                       This is something you should discuss with your players
                    ahead of time. Do they want to think about such things in
                    their game at all? Or would they prefer to keep the focus on
                    the adventure?
                       Romance can add a lot of fun to a game, even if it’s not
                    the primary focus. Such relationships tend to ground a
                    character and help them keep in perspective what’s most
                    important to them. They can also be the source of a great
                    deal of friction, especially if the character is keeping their
                    activities as a hero a secret.
                    Rivals
                    Many heroes have people they compete with not just during
                    their super-powered adventures but also in their regular
                    lives. Such rivals can cause the hero all sorts of headaches in
                    their occupations, their romances and in other parts of their
                    lives. They can also spur the character to greater heights in
                    an effort to equal or even surpass their rivals.
                        Sometimes rivalries can turn into friendships or romantic
                    relationships, and vice versa. These turns can add great
                    drama to your adventures and make them feel more real.
Michael Syrett (Order #53194700)
      Everyone Else
      If you like, you can also think about other people the
      characters are likely to interact with, especially if they’re
      liable to recur. This can be anyone from the clerk at the nearest
      bodega to a favorite bartender or a pair of police detectives.
          Spending a little time coming up with a name and a short
      description for such folks can add a lot to the game. Every
      time a character crops back up, it reminds the players of the
      history they have with them and makes their adventures
      feel more grounded.
      OTHER HEROES
      Beyond the regular people in the characters’ lives, they’re
      bound to run into all sorts of other super heroes. They’re
      likely to get to know some of them well—and not just among
      their teammates.
          If these characters become involved with the players’
      characters on a regular basis, you need to keep their presence
      in mind when cra ing your adventures and encounters.
      Otherwise, they can throw off the balance that you seek.
      Teammates
      While most of the players’ teammates are sure to be controlled
      by the other players in the game, that doesn’t have to be the
      end of them. For instance, if the characters are members of
      the Avengers or the X-Men, there are literally dozens of other
      super heroes who can claim a connection to them through
      those teams.
          Most of the time, you only need to focus on the characters
      your players control, but feel free to bring in others when
      you like. They can offer all kinds of support in terms of
      knowledge, experience or comradery. They can also serve
      as friends, rivals and even romantic interests.
          If you find yourself short a player or two for your planned
      adventure, you can always dra in an extra character or two
      to fight alongside the heroes. In such a case, you should play
      these support heroes as part of your duties, but you can let
      the other players give them directions or orders as seems fit.
      Mentors
      Sometimes the heroes might need a little advice from wiser
      folks who have been at this super-hero gig a bit longer than
      them. You can create new heroes to act as their mentors if
      you like, or you can tap the vast cast of Marvel heroes to
      bring in an existing hero instead.
          Even if the heroes are playing original characters, they
      might appreciate the chance to get advice from someone
      like a Captain America (any of them) or Professor X. In this
      way, you can help guide the heroes where they need to go,
      and you also cement the fact that the heroes are becoming
      an important part of your corner of the Marvel Multiverse.
      Leaders
      Some teams have natural leaders who rise to the top and help
                                                                          /10/ NARRATOR
      direct the rest of the team in times of crisis. Others never
      seem to gel that way. If you think your heroes could use a
      firmer hand, you can assign them a leader.
         This is a wonderful way to put the heroes in a position
      where they can be assigned missions by leaders who have the
      sort of information the characters wouldn’t otherwise have.
      They could, for instance, be government agents working in
303
===PDFPAGE 305===
                  /10/ NARRATOR
                 conjunction with their nation’s intelligence service for the
                 betterment of their country.
                    Leaders don’t always join their teams in the field, and
                 you can handle things like that as well. That allows you to
                 help the characters with the narrative parts of the adventure
                 while leaving the combat to them as the boots on the ground.
                 Sidekicks
                 Sometimes heroes wind up with other characters who hang
                 around and try to help them as best they can: sidekicks.
                 Traditionally, these are younger, lower-rank characters who
                 wouldn’t be able to survive many adventures on their own,
                 but they can still support the heroes in other ways, even if
                 that’s just taking over the communications system so the
                 heroes can focus on more pressing matters.
                    While the players may work alongside the sidekicks—and
                 may even fight alongside them at times—the Narrator should
                 remain in final control of them. Many sidekicks listen to their
                 hero pals and obey instructions from them, but sometimes
                 they don’t. When that happens, what they do instead isn’t
                 up to the other players but to you.
                 Animal/Robot Partners
                 A few heroes have helpers who aren’t even human. This
                 includes animals, robots and other creatures, like Mister
                 Fantastic’s lab assistant H.E.R.B.I.E. or Captain America (Sam
                 Wilson)’s falcon Redwing.
                     If such a character is going to be an integral part of a
                 character’s life, following them around and helping them
                 out, the player should fill out a character sheet for them and
                 keep that sheet with their regular character. However, just
                 as with sidekicks, mentors, leaders and so on, that partner
                 isn’t under the player’s direct control. They are likely to do
                 whatever the player’s character asks or orders them to do,
                 but they make their own decisions—which means you get
                 to decide for them as the Narrator when necessary.
                 VILLAINS
                 Aer their teammates, family and friends, the most important
                 people in a super hero’s life are the villains. They represent
                 the hero’s biggest threats and their greatest challenges.
                 Because of that, you should make sure to match your good
                 guys against the right bad guys.
                 Choosing Villains
                 If the players have chosen existing Marvel characters for their
                 heroes, this part should be easy. You can just inflict each hero’s
                 biggest villains upon them. If the players are working with
                 disparate characters from a number of different teams, the
                 villains may find themselves teaming up with other villains
                 they’ve never met in the comics, but those kinds of team-ups
                 are all part of the fun. You can use them for coming up with
                 fresh new plots that you haven’t seen in the comics as well.
                      Even if the players have created original characters, you
                 should still feel free to plunder the entirety of Marvel stories
                 for villains to pit them against. Lots of players get a big thrill
                 out of facing off against those classic opponents. They come
                 complete with their own histories and personalities, which
                 can be terribly handy.
                      Don’t let any of that stop you from coming up with your
                 own original villains if you like. Why should the other
Michael Syrett (Order #53194700)
      players have all that kind of fun? You can make up as many
      mysterious baddies as you need and fit them exactly to your
      adventures’ plots.
      Individual Enemies
      Many Marvel heroes have their own individual enemies who
      they’ve built up histories with over the course of decades.
      Even when those heroes are working with teams to defeat
      a greater menace, those personal foes can get to them on a
      level that other villains can’t reach.
          It’s the clash between these titans that defi nes them.
      That’s why they work so well together in their stories—and
      why they’re so easily able to get underneath each other’s skin.
          Think of matchups like Spider-Man versus the Green
      Goblin, Black Panther versus Killmonger, Captain America
      versus the Red Skull, Thor versus Loki and Professor X versus
      (and later working alongside) Magneto. That’s the level of
      conflict you’re looking for.
          The heroes in your game deserve the same. If you like, you
      can work with them to figure out the villains that they prefer
      the most. You don’t have to use the villains they prefer, of course,
      but you should at least consider using them in your adventures.
          Ideally, these villains are the same rank as the heroes. If
      they’re not, they should either have a number of underlings on
      their side, or they should team up with enough other villains to
      present the hero with a problem. A classic example of this is the
      Sinister Six, a group of villains who team up to fight Spider-Man
      (Peter Parker). In some cases, they’re too much for Spider-Man
      to handle on his own, which is when it’s time to call for help.
      Group Nemeses
      Super-hero teams tend to have their own nemeses as well.
      These are usually villains so powerful that no individual
      hero could hope to stand against them.
          Sometimes, those nemeses are a single person, like Kang
      the Conqueror. Other times, they’re an entire group of villains,
      like the Brotherhood of Mutants or the Masters of Evil. The
      only real criteria is that no individual member of the super-
      hero team is likely able to stand against them on their own.
      That’s why they belong to a team in the first place—so they
      can handle threats like this.
         Again, you have decades of Marvel villains you can tap for
      this purpose. You can find such villains mostly in the team
      books, facing off against groups of super heroes just like yours.
         When coming up with a single nemesis for a team, you
      should make them as tough as if not tougher than any single
      hero on the team. Generally, they should be a rank if not two
      higher. Major villains like these oen have lots of resources
      to draw upon as well, whether in the form of weaponry,
      technology or underlings. In fact, their underlings would
      oen make great villains on their own, but for the fact that
      they’ve teamed up under the lead villain’s guidance to take
      on teams like that of your heroes.
      Ranking Villains Up
      If you’re playing with heroes already at their rank cap,
      you don’t have to worry about advancing the villains at
      all. However, if the heroes are growing in rank, you should
      consider improving your villains to keep up with them. That
      way, they can maintain their adversarial relationship with
      the villains rather than leaving them behind.
304
===PDFPAGE 306===
                       If you like, you can instead use the heroes’ advancing in
                    rank to show how much tougher they are against their old
                    foes, who are stuck at the same rank. However, the heroes
                    should then fi nd themselves plagued by new and more
                    powerful villains than they’ve ever faced before.
                    RANK X
                    Some characters—whether heroes, villains or something
                    else—are too powerful to fit into the ranking system. They
                    make the regular Marvel characters—even the ones at Rank
                    6—seem puny and helpless by comparison.
Michael Syrett (Order #53194700)
           This includes characters like Galactus and the Beyonders
       as well as the Living Tribunal and various personifications
       of different abstract concepts, like Death, Eternity, Infinity
       and Oblivion. Rather than give them a rank and full statistics,
       we refer to them as Rank X.
           This doesn’t mean that the heroes can’t stand against
       such powerful characters or even try to attack them. It’s
       just that the solution to any problem that they have with
       them is more likely to be found narratively than in a fight.
           You can include such characters in your adventures,
       but you should always take care with them. Facing down
       beings of such immense power can be a heady experience,
       much different than stopping bank robbers or even a global
       invasion. It helps if you have a deep understanding of the
       underpinnings of the Marvel Multiverse.
           While encounters with Rank X beings can make the
       heroes feel small and insignificant, they can take comfort in
       the fact that they even had a rare meeting with such a being
       at all. Few people manage to do so and return to talk about it.
       MONOLOGUING
       Characters who do not have the Heroic tag don’t have a
       starting level of Karma. However, they can earn it by doing
       things that would normally earn Karma for any character,
       and they can then spend it just like Heroic characters can.
           One way that villains like to earn Karma is by
       monologuing. They stand before the heroes—or anyone else
       who might work against them—and deliver a speech that
       explains something about them. This could be the details
       of their current plan, but it just as well could include stories
       from their past that illuminate their motivation or asides
       that delve into their overarching philosophy.
           This is the chance for the villain to make the heroes listen
       to them, oen in an attempt to earn their respect. In game
       terms, they do this so they can earn Karma. They can then
         spend that Karma later to put their plan into action or—if
           everything goes wrong—to escape justice.
                Heroes can put a stop to a villain earning Karma in
            this way by interrupting their speech and putting an
            end to it. This is sure to infuriate the villain, of course,
             which can lead to great moments in their ongoing
             conflict with the heroes.
                 If you like, you can allow heroes to indulge in a
               monologue as well, but giving such a speech should be
                  even rarer for them. Monologues can quickly become
                     tedious if characters are allowed to deliver them
                        regularly. However, given at the right time and
                           the right place with the right audience, a
                             good monologue can reveal a great deal
                                 about a character, move the listeners
                                   to their core and make heroes out
                                      of those who hear them and take
                                         them to heart.

                    GLOSSARY/INDEX
                    A
                    Abilities 18–19, 44
                    Characters have six different abi lities:
                    Melee, Agility, Resilience, Vigilance, Ego
                    and Logic.
                    Ability Cap 44
                    The highest a character’s ability score can
                    be. The default is the character’s rank +3.
                    Ability Defense 19, 44
                    The target number for an action check
                    against that ability. To calculate this, add
                    +10 to a character’s ability score.
                    Ability Scores 18–19, 44–45, 48
                    How good a character is with one of the six
                    abilities. For most characters, these range
                    from –3 to +3. Super heroes can have much
                    higher scores.
                    Ablaze 37
                    The character is on fire. They lose 5 Health
                    at the end of each of their turns until the
                    fire is put out. An Agility check against a
                    target number of 10 can do this.
                    Action 28–31
                    Thing a character can do during their
                    turn, usually with a standard action or a
                    reaction.
                    Action Check 11–13
                    A d616 roll to determine if a character
                    succeeds at something. If it meets or beats
                    the target number, it succeeds.
                    Action Maneuvers 29–31
                    Things a character can do with an action.
                    Includes attack, dodge, escape, grab, help,
                    move and using a power.
                    B
                    Backstory 20, 45, 51–66
                    The character’s origin and occupation,
                    each of which gives them a set of traits
                    and tags.
                    Basic Power 20, 75, 80
                    A power that does not belong to a
                    power set.
                    Bleeding 37
                    The character is severely wounded. They
                    lose 5 Health at the end of each of their
                    turns. A Logic check against a target num-
                    ber of 10 can stop this, as can anything
                    that causes the character to recover at
                    least 1 Health.
                    Blinded 37
                    Any powers that require sight end. The
                    character’s speed is reduced by half. They
                    have trouble on action checks that require
                    sight, and enemies have an edge on all
                    action checks against them that require
                    sight to defend against.

                 H
                 Healing 36
                 A character who is not dead or shattered
                 regains lost Health and Focus equal to their
                 rank every hour they take it easy. For every
                 hour they sleep, they regain double that.
                 Health 19
                 A measure of the character’s physical
                 fortitude.
                 Health Damage 31
                 Damage done to a character’s Health. A
                 character with 0 Health is unconscious. A
                 character who has lost double their Health
                 is dead.
                 Holding a Turn 29
                 A character delays their turn until later in
                 a round.
                 I
                 Illusion 69, 281
                 A false image, usually created by magic or
                 technology.
                 Initiative 27
                 The order in which the characters involved
                 in a combat act. Higher numbers go first.
                 Initiative Check 27
                 A special action check each character in
                 a combat makes at the start to determine
                 the order in which they take their actions.
                 Initiative Modifier 27
                 The character’s Vigilance score, which is
                 added to their initiative check.
                 K
                 Karma 19
                 A measure of the character’s luck, equal to
                 the character’s rank.
                 Killed 36
                 The character is dead. Under special cir-
                 cumstances, characters have been known
                 to return from this state.
                 Knockback 34
                 If a character with the Mighty power gets
                 a Fantastic success on a close attack, they
                 can knock their target back 5 spaces for
                 every damage multiplier.
                 L
                 Label 51
                 A trait or a tag.
                 Line of Sight 27
                 A line drawn between an attacker and a
                 target to determine if the attacker can
                 see the target. Under good conditions, the
                 maximum is about 200 spaces.
                 M
                 Marvel Die 11
                 The differentiated die in a d616 roll. If you ro
                 a 1 on it (or a Marvel logo on specially designe
                 Marvel dice), you get a Fantastic result.

                    Spaces 20
                    On a map/board, a space equals 5 feet.
                    Special Effect 13–14
                    An extra effect certain kinds of powers
                    have on Fantastic successes.
                    Speed 20, 31–32
                    How fast a character can move in a round,
                    using a given movement mode, listed
                    in spaces.
                    Stacking 15, 34, 81
                    When elements in the game add their
                    effects together—which they generally
                    don’t. Powers and other effects that
                    increase or reduce damage do not stack.
                    Instead, the strongest one takes effect
                    while the others function as backups.
                    Standard Action 29
                    An action that requires most of a charac-
                    ter’s attention, like attacking. Most charac-
                    ters get one standard action each turn.
                    Stunned 38
                    Any powers the character is concentrating on
                    end immediately. They cannot use any actions,
                    and all attacks against them have an edge.
                    Success 13–14
                    An action check result that meets or beats
                    the target number.
                    Surprised 28, 38
                    Characters who are surprised by their
                    opponents when combat starts cannot act
                    in the bonus round.
                       If a character is surprised later in the
                    combat, the characters who surprised
                    them have an edge on attacks against
                    them for 1 round.
                    T
                    Tags 51, 63–65
                    Minor narrative elements that help
                    define a character but have no inherent
                    mechanic. A tag that challenges a charac-
                    ter during play can earn them Karma.

                                                   Enter The Multiverse!
                          Take on the roles of Marvel’s most famous Super Heroes—or create entirely new ones of your own—and put an
                          end to the sinister plots of the most menacing Super Villains in the Marvel Multiverse! The Marvel Multiverse Role-
                          Playing Game: Core Rulebook features all the rules you need to play. Including quick character creation, bombastic
                          combat, and scores of amazing powers plus full profiles of dozens of Marvel’s greatest heroes and villains.
                          Written by New York Times-bestseller Matt Forbeck (The Marvel Encyclopedia, Dungeons & Dragons: Dungeonology),
                          featuring full-page illustrations by Mike Bowden and art from Marvel’s vast library of comics, this book, three
                          standard dice and some friends are all you need to get started. The Marvel Multiverse is calling! Come join the fun!
